title: Heat on the move: why smoke rises and the Sun warms you across empty space

summary.text: Hold your palm beside a burning diya and it feels warm. Hold it a hand's width above, and it feels far hotter. Yet air is a poor carrier of heat, and the Sun's warmth reaches your face across millions of kilometres where there is no air at all. Your child watches hot and cold drops of coloured water go opposite ways in one glass, shields a palm from a flame with a card, and tests which wrapping lets the Sun warm a tumbler most. They find two new ways heat travels, convection and radiation. They follow both from a boiling pot to sea breezes, the Sun's bubbling surface and a candle flame that turns into a ball in space.
summary.art: A lit diya on a steel plate, with a child's palm held beside it and another palm held above it, and a thin card standing between the flame and the side palm.

intro.hook: Hold your hand beside a lit diya, 10 centimetres away. It feels warm. Now hold a card between the flame and your hand. The warmth stops at once. But hold your hand above the flame and the card beside it changes nothing. Why does the card block one kind of warmth but not the other?
intro.text: Last year you saw that heat creeps through a steel spoon from part to part. That is conduction. But air barely carries heat that way, and the Sun's warmth crosses empty space where there is nothing to creep through. So heat must have other ways to travel. In this unit you find them. You send hot and cold drops through a glass of water, you spin a paper spiral with rising air, and you test which wrapping lets the Sun warm a tumbler the most.
intro.art: A child at a table with a lit diya, a thin card standing upright between the flame and one hand, and the other hand held above the flame.

outcomes: I can name the three ways heat travels, conduction, convection and radiation, and show each one with something at home.
I can explain why warm air and warm water rise and cool air and water sink, and why this makes a loop called a convection current.
I can explain how a sea breeze, a rising kite bird, a chimney and the monsoon winds all come from convection.
I can explain that radiation carries heat with nothing to travel through, which is how the Sun's heat crosses empty space.
I can explain why dark, dull things take in more radiation than pale, shiny things, and why a white roof keeps a house cooler.
I can make a prediction with a reason, plan a fair test, and say what my results show and what they do not.
I can look at a new situation and say which ways heat is travelling, and when more than one is working at once.
I can explain why 'heat rises' and 'cold comes in' are not quite right, and say what is really happening.

terms.meaning: Heat passing from one part of a solid to the next part that touches it.
terms.example: A steel ladle standing in hot sambar slowly warms all the way up its handle.
terms.art: A steel ladle standing in a pot, with small arrows climbing up the handle.

terms.meaning: Heat carried from place to place by a moving liquid or gas.
terms.example: Hot rasam rises in the middle of the pot and cooler rasam sinks at the sides.
terms.art: A pot of boiling water seen from the side, with arrows rising in the middle and sinking at the edges.

terms.meaning: Heat that travels as invisible light-like waves, and needs nothing to travel through.
terms.example: You feel the warmth of a bonfire on your face even when the air around you is cold.
terms.art: A child sitting beside a bonfire, with wavy lines going from the fire to the child's face.

terms.meaning: Anything that can flow, which means any liquid or any gas.
terms.example: Water, oil and air are all fluids.
terms.art: A glass of water, a bottle of oil and a puff of air from a balloon side by side.

terms.example: Air in a balloon expands when you warm it.
terms.art: A small balloon beside a warm cup and the same balloon bigger after being warmed.

terms.meaning: How much stuff is packed into a space. A dense thing is heavy for its size.
terms.example: A steel katori is denser than the same size of water.
terms.art: Two equal boxes, one packed with many dots and one with a few dots.

terms.meaning: A loop of moving fluid, rising where it is warm and sinking where it is cool.
terms.example: In a pot of boiling water, the water goes up in the middle, across the top, down at the sides and round again.
terms.art: A glass of water on a flame with a loop of arrows going up, across, down and back.

terms.meaning: A column of warm air rising from hot ground.
terms.example: Black kites circle on a thermal above a hot road without flapping.
terms.art: A black kite bird circling in the sky above a hot road, with wavy arrows rising from the road.

terms.meaning: A wind that blows from the cool sea onto the warm land during the day.
terms.example: On the Marina beach in Chennai, the afternoon wind comes in from the sea.
terms.art: A beach in the afternoon with arrows from the sea to the land and warm air rising over the land.

terms.meaning: Light our eyes cannot see, which carries most of the heat we feel from warm things.
terms.example: A heater glowing dull red also sends out a lot of infrared that you feel as warmth.
terms.art: A thermal camera picture of a hand, with the warm hand shown in yellow and the cool background in blue.

terms.meaning: To take in. A thing that absorbs radiation takes it in and gets warmer.
terms.example: A black school bag absorbs sunlight and gets hot.
terms.art: A black bag in sunlight with arrows going into it.

terms.meaning: To bounce back. A thing that reflects radiation sends it away and stays cooler.
terms.example: A white roof reflects most of the sunlight that lands on it.
terms.art: A white roof in sunlight with arrows bouncing off it.

terms.meaning: A material that carries heat very slowly. Still air that cannot circulate is one.
terms.example: A woollen shawl keeps you warm by holding still air against your skin.
terms.art: A child wrapped in a shawl, with small pockets of air drawn in the wool.

terms.meaning: A wind that blows from the cooler land out to the warmer sea at night.
terms.example: A fishing boat can leave a beach before dawn with the wind behind it.
terms.art: A beach at night with arrows from the land out to the sea and warm air rising over the sea.

terms.meaning: Anything that gives out more heat than it takes in, such as a flame, the Sun or a hot stove.
terms.example: A lit gas burner is the heat source for a pot of dal.
terms.art: A gas burner with a flame under a pot, and a few arrows leaving the flame.

explanations.description: In Class 3 you met conduction. A steel spoon in hot tea warms up its handle because each tiny part of the steel passes its jiggling to the next. But conduction needs something to touch, and it is slow. So heat has two more ways. Convection works in liquids and gases, which can flow. The hot part moves, and takes its heat along. Radiation does not need anything at all. A bonfire warms your face by sending out waves that cross the cold air and the air does not carry them. Most real things use more than one way at once. A pot of dal on a stove is warmed by conduction through the base, by convection in the dal, and by radiation to your face if you lean over it.
examples: A steel ladle in hot sambar warms its handle by conduction.
Rice grains rising and falling in a boiling pot show convection.
The warmth on your face from a bonfire is radiation.
explanations.art: A pot on a stove with three coloured arrows: one up the ladle handle, one looping round in the water, and one in wavy lines to a child's face.
explanations.definition: Heat travels from a hotter place to a cooler place in three ways. Conduction passes it from part to touching part. Convection carries it in a moving liquid or gas. Radiation sends it as invisible waves that need nothing to travel through.

explanations.concept: Why warm air and warm water rise
explanations.description: Heat makes the tiny particles in a fluid move faster, and they push a little further apart. The same amount of stuff now takes up more room, so each spoonful is lighter than before. That is what less dense means. Air that is warmed from 27 to 57 degrees Celsius becomes about a tenth lighter. Water warmed from 20 to 60 degrees becomes about one and a half in a hundred lighter. Surrounded by cooler, heavier fluid, the warm part is lifted, the same way a cork is lifted in water. Cooler fluid does not rise. It sinks, and that sinking is what pushes the warm fluid up. Water has one odd habit. Between 4 and 0 degrees it gets lighter again as it gets colder, which is part of why ice floats and why a lake freezes from the top.
examples: Smoke from an agarbatti curls upwards in still air.
A hot-air balloon rises because the air inside is less dense than the air outside.
Steam from an idli cooker climbs to the ceiling.
explanations.art: Two equal boxes of dots, one with the dots close together and one with them spread out, and a cork-like rising arrow on the spread-out one.
explanations.definition: When a liquid or gas is warmed, it expands and becomes less dense. The cooler fluid around it is heavier, so it sinks and pushes the lighter warm fluid up.

explanations.concept: A convection current is a loop
explanations.description: Warm fluid cannot rise forever, because there is nowhere for it to go. It has to spread out at the top and cool. Once it is cooler it is heavier, so it sinks. At the bottom it is drawn back towards the heat. So the up and the down are not two things. They are one loop that keeps itself going for as long as the heat lasts. You can see a loop in a pot of boiling water, because rice grains ride it up the middle and down the sides. A rooftop solar water heater in India works the same way. Water heated in the black panel rises into the tank, and cool water sinks down to take its place, with no pump at all. A fridge freezer sits at the top for the same reason. The air it cools sinks and chills the food below.
examples: Rice grains circling in a boiling pot.
A rooftop solar water heater, where hot water collects at the top of the tank.
The freezer box at the top of a single-door fridge.
explanations.art: A glass of water over a flame, with a loop of arrows going up the middle, across the top, down both sides and back along the bottom.
explanations.definition: A convection current is a loop. Fluid warms and rises in one place, spreads along the top and cools, sinks in another place, and flows back along the bottom to be warmed again.

explanations.description: Land warms and cools quickly. The sea warms and cools slowly, because it is deep and the water mixes. On a sunny afternoon the land is hotter, so air over it rises. Cooler air from over the sea slides in underneath to take its place. This is the sea breeze, and it is why the Marina beach in Chennai is pleasant in the evening. At night the land cools below the sea and the loop runs the other way, as a land breeze. Sailors and fishing communities around the world have used both winds, leaving with the land breeze and coming home with the sea breeze. Birds do the same with a thermal. Black kites in Indian cities circle upwards on rising warm air above hot roads and roofs, without flapping. Part of the monsoon works like a sea breeze that lasts for months, as the land heats up through the summer and pulls in moist air from the Indian Ocean. The full story has more in it, such as the Himalaya and ocean currents.
examples: A sea breeze on Kozhikode beach in the afternoon.
A black kite bird circling over a hot tin roof in Madurai.
The summer monsoon winds, partly pulled in by the heating land.
explanations.art: A coast with a hot land on the left and a cool sea on the right, and a loop of arrows rising over the land, flowing back along the top and sinking over the sea.
explanations.definition: The same loop works at every size. On a beach in the day, land warms faster than sea, so air rises over the land and cool sea air flows in as a sea breeze. At night the land cools faster and the wind turns round.

explanations.concept: Convection inside the Earth and the Sun
explanations.description: Under the Earth's thin crust, the mantle is made of hot rock that is so squeezed that it flows very slowly, a few centimetres a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow. Hotter rock rises and cooler rock sinks, in giant slow loops. On the Sun, the surface is covered in bubbles of hot gas called granules, each about 1,000 kilometres across, rising and sinking in about ten minutes. This is the same loop as in a pot of boiling dal, at a size that is almost too big to picture.
examples: The Sun's surface looks like boiling rice when it is photographed up close.
The mantle under India flows very slowly beneath the plate that carries us northwards.
explanations.art: A cut-away of the Earth with slow loops of arrows inside the mantle, and beside it a close-up of the Sun's grainy surface.

perspectives.explanation: The cold, heavy edge of a plate sinks into the mantle and pulls the rest of the plate after it. On this view the sinking part of the loop is what moves the plates.

perspectives.who: Geologists who stress the mantle's flow
perspectives.explanation: The slow currents of rock under the plates drag them along like a conveyor belt. Most geologists today think both ideas are partly true, and they are still working out how much each one counts.

explanations.definition: Convection also happens in solid-looking rock deep inside the Earth, and in the glowing gas at the Sun's surface. Scientists agree that both happen. They still argue about how much the Earth's slow rock currents move the plates on the surface.

explanations.concept: Radiation: heat that needs nothing to travel through
explanations.description: A hot thing sends out energy as waves. The waves are a kind of light, and the part that carries most of the warmth you feel is called infrared. We cannot see it, but we feel it on our skin. These waves need nothing to carry them. They travel through air, through glass and through the empty space between the Sun and the Earth, which is about 150 million kilometres. Light and warmth from the Sun take about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to arrive. Every warm thing sends out infrared, and that includes you. A person sitting still gives out about as much heat as an old 100 watt bulb. A thermal camera shows this as colour. Some snakes, including pythons and pit vipers, have small pits that sense infrared, so they can find a warm mouse in the dark. In India, the physicist Anna Mani, who was born in Kerala in 1918, led the building of instruments at the India Meteorological Department in Pune to measure sunshine and solar radiation across the country.
examples: The Sun warming your face on the terrace.
The warmth you feel standing near a hot tandoor with no touching.
A thermal camera picture of a crowded classroom.
explanations.art: The Sun and the Earth far apart with wavy lines crossing a dark empty space between them, and a tiny clock showing 8 minutes.
explanations.definition: Radiation is energy carried by waves of light, including light our eyes cannot see. All warm things send it out, and it can cross empty space.

explanations.concept: Dark and light, shiny and dull
explanations.description: A black cloth in the Sun takes in nearly all the light that falls on it, and turns it into heat. A white cloth sends much of it back. A sheet of kitchen foil, with its shiny side out, reflects almost all the infrared that lands on it. That is why a solar cooker has a shiny reflector, why rescue blankets are silver, and why a thermos has silver walls. There is a second half to the rule. The things that are best at taking in radiation are also best at giving it out. A black pot cools quickly once it leaves the stove, and a shiny one stays hot for longer. In Ahmedabad, some families in hot, crowded neighbourhoods paint their tin roofs white to reflect the Sun, and the rooms below can be a few degrees cooler.
examples: A black school bag gets hotter than a white one in the Sun.
A white-painted terrace stays cooler than a bare dark one.
A silver thermos holds hot chai warm for hours.
explanations.art: Sunlight falling on a black roof and a white roof side by side, with most arrows bouncing off the white one and most going into the black one.
explanations.definition: When radiation lands on a thing, it can be absorbed, reflected, or pass through. Dark, dull things absorb the most and get warmest. White and shiny things reflect the most and stay coolest.

explanations.concept: Which way is the heat really going?
explanations.description: When you open a fridge, it feels as if the cold comes out. But what is really happening is that warm air from the kitchen goes in, and cool, heavy air from inside spills out and slides along the floor. The heat is going into the fridge, not the cold out of it. A steel plate feels colder than a wooden board in the same room because steel takes heat out of your hand faster. Likewise, 'heat rises' is not quite right. Hot air rises and hot water rises. But heat in a solid spoon travels in every direction, including downwards, and radiation goes out in every direction at once.
examples: Opening a fridge door on a hot day.
A steel tumbler of cold water, which warms up from the room around it.
A hot spoon laid flat that still warms its whole handle.
explanations.art: A fridge with its door open and arrows of warm room air going in and a cool heavy cloud spilling along the floor.
explanations.definition: Heat always moves from a hotter place to a cooler place. There is no cold stuff that moves. When something feels cold, heat is moving out of you into it.

explanations.concept: A flame in space is a ball
explanations.description: On Earth a candle flame is shaped like a teardrop, because the hot gas around it is lighter and rises, and fresh air flows in underneath to feed the flame. In the weightlessness of a spacecraft, nothing is heavier or lighter in the way that matters, so nothing is pushed up and fresh air does not flow in. NASA and other space agencies have burned candles in space, and the flame is a small, dim, blue ball. It only burns because oxygen slowly drifts in by itself. It is why the station has fans running all day. Without them, an astronaut's own breath would collect in a bubble round their face while they slept.
examples: Candle flame experiments on the space station, run by NASA.
The fans on the space station that keep air moving.
A candle flame on Earth with its tall teardrop shape.
explanations.art: Two candle flames side by side: a tall teardrop flame on Earth and a small round blue ball in a spacecraft.
explanations.definition: Convection needs gravity. Where nothing falls, as in a spacecraft, hot air does not rise, so a candle flame becomes a small round ball and many fires go out.

explanations.concept: Using all three: keeping cool and keeping warm
explanations.description: Old Chettinad houses in Tamil Nadu have a central open courtyard and tall wooden ventilators high on the walls. Hot air collects under the roof and leaves through the top, and cooler shaded air from the courtyard flows in low down. Convection does the work. A woollen shawl, a quilt and a double-glass window work the other way. They hold a layer of still air that cannot circulate, and still air is a very poor conductor and cannot carry heat by convection either. A thermos uses all three ideas. It has two walls with nothing between them, so no conduction and no convection, and silver coating on the walls to reflect radiation.
examples: The high ventilators in an old Chettinad house.
A white-painted roof in Ahmedabad.
A woollen shawl in a Kashmir winter.
explanations.art: A cut-away of a courtyard house with cool air flowing in low from the courtyard and hot air rising out through a high ventilator.
explanations.definition: To keep a place cool, block radiation with a white or shiny roof and let rising hot air leave through high openings. To keep a place warm, trap still air, because air that cannot move carries heat very slowly.

agreed.text: Heat flows by itself only from a hotter place to a cooler place.
agreed.evidence: No one has seen it flow the other way on its own. A cold tumbler in a warm room always warms, and a hot tumbler always cools.

agreed.text: When a fluid is warmed, it expands and becomes less dense, so it rises through the cooler fluid around it.
agreed.evidence: The densities of water and air have been measured at many temperatures, and they match what hot and cold drops of dye do in a glass.

agreed.text: Radiation can carry heat across empty space.
agreed.evidence: The Sun's warmth reaches the Earth through about 150 million kilometres of nearly empty space, and spacecraft are warmed by sunlight where there is no air.

agreed.text: Dark, dull surfaces absorb more radiation than light, shiny ones.
agreed.evidence: Thermometers in sunlight rise most under black covers and least under shiny foil, in many tests since the 1800s.

agreed.text: Every object above absolute zero sends out infrared radiation.
agreed.evidence: Thermal cameras read it from people, animals, buildings and stars.

agreed.text: A sea breeze blows onto the land in the day because the land warms faster than the sea.
agreed.evidence: Weather stations along coasts record the wind turning towards the land in late morning and back at night.

challenging.for: Smoke, steam and hot-air balloons all rise.
challenging.against: Hot fluids rise, but heat itself goes in every direction. A hot spoon warms downwards as well as upwards, and radiation goes out sideways and down.

challenging.claim: Cold flows into a room when you open a window in winter.
challenging.for: It feels as if cold air pours in and cold air does move in.
challenging.against: There is no cold stuff. Heat flows out of the warm room to the cold outside, and the cold air that comes in is just air that has less heat.

challenging.claim: Heat is a weightless fluid called caloric that flows from hot things to cold things.
challenging.who: Many scientists of the 1700s, including Antoine Lavoisier.
challenging.for: It explained why heat flows from hot to cold, and why heat seemed to pass through things.
challenging.against: Count Rumford saw in 1798 that boring a cannon made heat without end, which a fixed amount of fluid could not do. Heat is energy of motion, and radiation is light.

challenging.claim: Heat and light are two completely different things that travel together in sunlight.
challenging.for: We feel heat and see light with different senses.
challenging.against: In 1800, William Herschel found that heat reached its peak just beyond the red end of sunlight spread out by a prism, where nothing was visible. Infrared turned out to be light our eyes cannot see.

challenging.claim: The Sun warms the air between the Sun and us, and the warm air warms us.
challenging.for: It feels warmer in the Sun than in the shade.
challenging.against: Radiation passes through clear air and mostly warms the ground and our skin. If it warmed the air in between, mountain tops, which are closer to the Sun, would be warmer, but they are colder.

challenging.claim: The slow currents of the Earth's mantle are what move the continents.
challenging.who: Arthur Holmes proposed it in 1931, and many geologists agree.
challenging.for: The mantle does convect, and plates do move.
challenging.against: Many geologists now think the pull of cold, heavy plate edges sinking into the mantle matters more than the mantle's flow underneath.

big_questions.q: In the Colour Currents test, hot water rose and cold water sank, in the same glass. Did the hot water go up by itself, or did the cold water push it up?
big_questions.hint: Think about what would happen if there were no cold water to sink.

big_questions.q: When you open the fridge, does the cold come out, or does the heat go in? How could you tell the difference?
big_questions.hint: Think of a cold drink left on the table. What happens to it, and which way does the heat go?

big_questions.q: A candle flame is a teardrop on Earth and a ball in space. What was the air doing around the flame all along?
big_questions.hint: Think about what rising air needs in order to rise.

big_questions.q: Nothing carries the Sun's heat across empty space. So what is heat?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a thermometer actually measures, and what the Sun sends us.

big_questions.q: Wind exists only because two places have different temperatures. If the whole Earth were one temperature, what would be left?
big_questions.hint: Think about sea breezes, the monsoon and ocean currents.

big_questions.q: A black kite circles for an hour without flapping. Who is doing the work, the bird or the Sun?
big_questions.hint: Follow the energy back from the bird's wings, step by step.

big_questions.q: In a hot city, some families live under tin roofs and some under thick concrete with trees outside. Who gets to be cool, and who decides?
big_questions.hint: Think about who can afford a white roof, a fan, a tree or an air conditioner.

big_questions.q: You give off heat all the time, about as much as a bright bulb. Where does it go, and where did it come from?
big_questions.hint: Follow the heat back to your last meal.

story.title: The House That Breathes
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real. Warm air collects near a roof and, if there is a high opening, it leaves, while cooler air comes in through a low opening. Old courtyard houses in the Chettinad region of Tamil Nadu were built with high ventilators and an open courtyard, which helps with this.
text: In April, when the heat in Karaikudi made the road shimmer, Meenakshi went to stay with her Paati. Paati's house was very old. It had a long front hall, thick walls, and in the middle an open square to the sky, which the family called the muttram. High up on the walls of the hall were tall wooden ventilators, carved with flowers. They were so far above the floor that Meenakshi had never seen anyone open or close them.
Outside, the afternoon was forty-one degrees. Inside the hall, it was always cooler. Meenakshi had never asked why.
Then Ravi Mama came from Chennai with a tape measure and a plan. He was Meenakshi's mother's brother, and he built flats for a living. He walked through the hall and shook his head.
'This house wastes cool air,' he said. 'I will put glass sheets over those high ventilators, shut the doors, and put one air conditioner in this hall. Then the cool stays in.'
Paati was cutting betel leaves. She did not look up. 'A house has to breathe, Ravi.'
Mama laughed. 'Houses do not breathe, Paati. Air is just air.'

Meenakshi said nothing. But that evening she took one agarbatti from the puja shelf and asked Paati if she could light it. She stood at the low side door that led to the muttram and held the glowing stick in the doorway. The smoke did not rise straight up. It leaned into the hall. It drifted along near the floor, as if somebody very small was walking it inside. Then, far across the hall, it began to climb, and it climbed all the way to the tall ventilator and slipped out through the carved flowers.
'Mama, look,' she said. 'The smoke goes in low and goes out high.'
'Smoke goes where it likes,' said Mama, and he went to find his ladder.

By Friday, every ventilator was covered with glass. The air conditioner was fitted in the hall, with a long cable running to the wall. Mama switched it on that evening and the room grew cold. He was very pleased with himself. Paati sat in the courtyard with her betel leaves and said nothing at all.

On Saturday, at two o'clock in the afternoon, the electricity went off. In Karaikudi that happens often in April. The air conditioner went silent. Mama closed all the doors, to keep in the cold that was left.

In half an hour the hall was like the inside of a closed car. The air did not move. Mama's shirt stuck to his back. He opened the main door, but still the hall stayed hot, and the heat seemed to be gathered under the roof like a thick blanket. He carried a chair out to the courtyard, where Paati sat in the shade, and sat down heavily.
'It is cooler out here,' he said. 'Why is it cooler out here, and not in there? The doors are open now.'
Meenakshi had been watching the hall. 'Mama, the hot air is trapped,' she said. 'It has gone up to the roof, and the glass is the lid. It is like the idli cooker with the lid on.'
'But the cooker has a vent,' said Mama.
'So did our hall,' said Meenakshi. 'You covered it.'

Mama was too hot to argue. He fetched the ladder and, with Meenakshi holding the bottom, he climbed up and lifted the glass off one tall ventilator. It was stiff, and he said some words that Paati pretended not to hear.

Then Meenakshi lit the agarbatti again and held it at the low door. The smoke leaned in, just as before. It walked along the floor. And then it rose, faster than before, and went up and out through the open ventilator like a thread being pulled.
A cool breath touched Mama's ankles. It came in from the muttram, low and slow, along the stone floor. He stood very still, the way people do when something has just become clear.

'The hot air is going up and out,' he said slowly. 'And that is why the cool air comes in below. It is not the hot air leaving by itself. It is the cool air, which is heavier, coming in underneath and pushing it up.'
'And it only works if there is a way out at the top and a way in at the bottom,' said Meenakshi.
Paati smiled and tied up her hair. 'I told you,' she said. 'A house has to breathe.'

That week, Mama took off every sheet of glass. He kept the air conditioner for the back bedroom, where the old house had no ventilator. And on the last day of his holiday, he stood in the hall at three o'clock, in the middle of a heat wave, with the carved flowers above him, and he was cool.
story.epiphany: Warm air does not leave a room by itself. The cooler, heavier air comes in low and pushes it up and out. A room needs an opening high up and an opening low down for this loop to work.
ask: Why does hot air collect under a roof, and what does it need to leave?
If the glass sheets had stayed on the ventilators, what would you expect to happen to the smoke from the agarbatti?
How could you use this idea to keep your own home cooler on a hot day, without a fan?
