items.b: Radiation. Heat crosses the cold air in straight lines, without the air carrying it.

items.f: Steam from an idli cooker drifts up to the kitchen ceiling.
items.b: Convection. Warm, damp air is lighter than the air around it, and it rises.

items.f: The iron handle of a tawa gets too hot to hold.
items.b: Conduction. Heat travels through the iron from the hot base to the handle.

items.f: A black kite bird circles higher and higher over a hot road, without flapping.
items.b: Convection. The hot road warms the air above it, and the rising air lifts the bird.

items.f: You hold your palm 10 centimetres beside a diya and feel warmth.
items.b: Radiation. The warmth reaches your palm in a straight line, and a card would block it.

items.f: A hot-air balloon rises when the burner is switched on.
items.b: Convection. The heated air inside is lighter than the cooler air outside, so the balloon rises.

items.f: A steel tumbler of hot chai burns your fingers when you pick it up.
items.b: Conduction. Heat passes from the chai through the steel into your fingers.

items.f: Cool air from an open fridge spills over your feet.
items.b: Convection. Cool air is heavier than warm air, so it sinks and spreads along the floor.

items.f: In the afternoon, a cool wind blows from the sea onto the Marina beach in Chennai.
items.b: Convection. Air rises over the warm land and cooler sea air flows in underneath.

items.f: A black school bag left in the Sun gets hotter than a white one.
items.b: Radiation. The dark bag takes in more of the Sun's radiation than the white one.

items.f: Sunlight reaches the Earth across 150 million kilometres of empty space.
items.b: Radiation. It is the only way heat can cross empty space, because there is nothing to touch or to flow.

items.f: The hot water in a rooftop solar heater collects at the top of the tank.
items.b: Convection. The hot water is lighter and rises, and cool water sinks to the panel to be heated.

items.f: You hold your hand above a steaming cup of tea and feel the warm, damp air.
items.b: Convection. The warm air rises from the cup and carries heat to your hand.

items.f: The thick copper base of a pan spreads the heat evenly from the flame.
items.b: Conduction. Copper is a very good conductor, so heat moves quickly through it.

items.f: A lamp 20 centimetres to the side of your cheek makes your skin feel warm.
items.b: Radiation. The warmth travels in a straight line from the bulb to your skin.

items.f: The smoke from an agarbatti curls upward and bends over.
items.b: Convection. The smoke is carried along by warm air rising from the stick.

items.f: A solar cooker with a shiny flap bakes food in the Sun.
items.b: Radiation. The shiny flap reflects sunlight into the box, where the black base absorbs it.

items.f: Hot air collects near the ceiling of a crowded hall.
items.b: Convection. Warm air from people is lighter, so it rises and gathers under the roof.

items.f: Milk on a stove: the bottom of the pan gets hot first, then all the milk warms up.
items.b: More than one. Heat conducts through the pan's base, and then convection stirs it through the milk.

items.f: A roti is held over an open gas flame with tongs and puffs up.
items.b: More than one. The flame sends radiation to the roti, and hot gases rise past it by convection.

items.f: Beach sand burns your feet at noon.
items.b: More than one. The Sun's radiation warmed the sand, and then conduction passes the heat into your feet.

items.f: A tandoor roti sticks to the hot clay wall and cooks.
items.b: More than one. The clay conducts heat into the dough, the hot air carries heat round it, and the glowing walls radiate heat.

printables.title: 16 tokens: four each of Conduction, Convection, Radiation and More than one

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player puts one token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. A player whose token matches the first words of the back scores one point.
A player who also says why, using the words hot, cool, light, heavy, touch or straight lines in a correct reason, scores one more point. The reader decides.
After each card, the reader's job passes to the player on the left.
With two players, swap the reader's job after every card. The reader does not guess on their own card.
Playing alone: read the front, choose a token, say your reason out loud, and then turn the card over. Score one point for a right answer and one for a right reason. Try to beat your own score.
The game ends when all 24 cards have been read. The player with the most points wins. If there is a tie, the tied players share the win.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the 16 tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. Give each player one token of each kind.
flow.say: These cards describe times when heat moves. Each player gets four tokens. Conduction, convection, radiation, and more than one. We will decide which one it was.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Each player takes four tokens.
flow.parent: Print the cards double-sided if you can, so the answer is on the back. If you have no printer, copy each card onto a slip of paper with the answer on the other side, or write the answers on a separate sheet and keep it hidden. A child cuts with a grown-up nearby. For 2 to 4 players the 16 tokens are enough, since the reader does not use tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Heat Detectives. You set up the cards and tokens.

flow.do: Play the first six cards. After each card, read the back aloud. After card three, ask the question below.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone else picks a token. Turn the tokens over together. Now the reader reads the back. Who got a point? Who can say why?
flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: What clue on the card tells you it is conduction?
good: Two things are touching.
The heat goes through a solid.
There is a spoon or a handle.

flow.parent: Look out for clues. Touching and solids mean conduction. Moving liquid or air means convection. Light, glow or an empty gap means radiation.
flow.context: In this step, you play the first six cards and learn how to score.

flow.do: Play the next ten cards. After card ten, stop and ask the question below.
flow.say: Keep playing. After each card, say your reason out loud before the reader turns it over. Which kind of card is the easiest? Which is the hardest?
flow.kid: Play the next ten cards. Say your reason out loud first.

ask.q: Which cards were tricky, and why?
good: The ones with more than one way.
The ones where I could not see the air moving.

flow.parent: The trickiest are the cards with more than one way. Heat often travels two or three ways at once, and one card can have several answers, but the back gives the biggest or most interesting one.
flow.context: In this step, you play more cards and learn to spot the clues.

flow.do: Play the last eight cards and add up the scores. Then ask your child to make up a card about something in your home. They say what the answer is.
flow.say: Play the last cards. Add up the points. Now make your own card. Think of something in our home where heat moves. What kind is it, and why?
flow.kid: Play the last cards. Add up the points. Make up your own card.
flow.parent: Write down their card and add it to the pile next time you play. Good cards come from the kitchen, the bathroom, the school bus or the terrace.
flow.think: Can you think of a time when heat moved in all three ways at once?
flow.context: This is the last step of Heat Detectives. You finish the game and invent a card.

experiments.title: Colour Currents: which way does a hot or cold drop travel?
experiments.question: A drop of red water goes into the middle of a glass of still, room-temperature water. Does it rise, sink or stay put? Does the answer change if the drop is hot, warm, room-temperature or ice-cold?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess what each of the four drops will do: hot, warm, room-temperature and ice-cold. Which will move fastest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every drop is the same red water, the same amount (one straw-full), and is let go at the same depth in a glass of still water of the same height. The water in the glass is always room temperature and always still for two minutes first. Only the temperature of the drop changes, so any difference comes from the temperature.
results_table: What it did: rose, sank or stayed
Seconds to reach the top or the bottom

materials.item: a clear glass tumbler (a plain 250 millilitre drinking glass is ideal). With 2 to 4 children, one glass each if you have them
4 small katoris or cups, each with about 50 millilitres of water
red food colouring (or a few drops of washable school ink or fountain-pen ink; strong tea or turmeric water is not good, because it smears)
4 plastic drinking straws (not the bendy kind)
a kettle of hot water, a jug of cold tap water and 3 ice cubes (or a cup of water kept in the fridge)
a piece of white paper or card to hold behind the glass
a phone or kitchen timer with seconds
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours all the hot water. The hot drop should be about 50 to 60 degrees: too hot to sip, but you can still hold the outside of the katori. Never suck on a straw that has hot water in it. The finger-over-the-end trick needs no sucking. Wipe spills at once, so nobody slips. Food colour and ink stain clothes, so wear an old shirt.
experiments.record: Fill in the table for each drop. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen (claim), what you saw (evidence), and why you think it happened (reasoning). Draw the glass with an arrow for each drop to show where it went.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you let go of four drops of red water at different temperatures in one glass of still water, and watch which way each one travels. This shows how heat moves in water.

setup.art: Four small katoris in a row on a table, labelled hot, warm, room and ice-cold, each with red water and a straw standing in it.
setup.caption: 1. Make four katoris of red water: hot, warm, room-temperature and ice-cold.

setup.art: A tall glass of clear water standing in front of a white card, with a ruler beside it showing the water 8 centimetres deep.
setup.caption: 2. Fill a glass with room-temperature water. Wait two minutes until it is perfectly still.

setup.art: A hand holding a straw full of red water with a finger over the top end, lowering the tip into the middle of the glass.
setup.caption: 3. Fill a straw from the first katori. Put a finger over the top. Lower the tip to the middle of the glass.

setup.art: A finger lifted off the end of the straw and a small red cloud spreading from the straw tip, with a timer in the picture.
setup.caption: 4. Lift your finger. Start the timer. Watch which way the red goes.

setup.art: A glass with a red stream curling upwards, and next to it a glass with a red stream sinking down, with the times written below each.
setup.caption: 5. Stop the timer when the red reaches the top or the bottom. Write down the seconds.

flow.do: Show your child the materials. Say that four drops will be let go in one glass. Ask for a guess and a reason for each drop. Write them down.
flow.say: We will let four drops of red water go in the same glass. One is hot, one is warm, one is room-temperature, and one is ice-cold. What will each drop do? Rise, sink or stay? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four red drops go in one glass. Hot, warm, room and ice-cold. What will each one do? Why?

ask.q: Which drop do you think will move fastest? Why?
good: The hottest, because it has the most heat.
The coldest, because it is heavy.
Maybe none will move.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Write each guess and its reason at the top of the table. Wrong guesses are useful, because they make the result a surprise.
flow.context: This is the first step of Colour Currents. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up makes the four katoris. Put 50 millilitres of water in each and 3 drops of red colour. Make one very hot, one warm like a bath, one room-temperature, and one ice-cold with ice cubes. Take the ice out.
flow.say: The grown-up makes four katoris of red water. One is hot, like tea you wait to sip. One is warm, like bath water. One is room-temperature. One is cold from the ice. Take the ice cubes out before you use it.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes four katoris of red water. Hot, warm, room and ice-cold.
flow.parent: Mix half kettle water and half cold tap water for the hot katori. It should be too hot to sip but safe to hold the outside of the katori. If you have a thermometer, about 55 degrees is right, but you do not need one. Use the same number of colour drops in each. If the red is too strong, use 2 drops. Too much colour can make the drop heavier than the water for a different reason. Keep the ice-cold katori in the fridge or with ice cubes for 10 minutes before you use it, and take the ice out just before you test, because floating ice cubes will make swirls. If you have no ice, a katori that has sat in the fridge overnight also works. Do the hot katori last, and keep it covered with a plate or saucer so it does not cool while you wait.

check.q: Why do all four katoris get the same red colour and the same amount of water?
options: So only the temperature is different
So the colour looks nice
So the water stays clear
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If one drop had more colour, it might sink or rise because of the colour, and we would not know whether the temperature was the cause.

flow.context: In this step, a grown-up makes the four temperatures of red water.

flow.do: Fill the glass with room-temperature tap water, to about 8 centimetres deep. Stand it in front of the white paper. Wait two minutes. Watch the water until nothing moves.
flow.say: Fill the glass with tap water. Wait two minutes. The water is still when you cannot see anything moving. Hold the white paper behind the glass so the red will show up well.
flow.kid: Fill the glass. Wait two minutes. Wait until the water is still.

ask.q: Why do we wait for the water to be still?
good: So no stirring moves the red drop.
So the only thing moving it is its temperature.

flow.parent: If the glass has been moved, tiny swirls hide the result. Wait until a dust speck or bubble stops moving. Use the same glass and the same depth every time.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the glass and wait for the water to be still.

flow.do: Test the drops one at a time, in this order: room-temperature, ice-cold, warm, hot. Fill a straw from the katori and press your finger on the top end. Lift it out. Lower the tip to the middle of the glass. Lift your finger and start the timer. Stop it when the red reaches the top or the bottom. Pour out the water and refill the glass. Wait two minutes between tests. (If you have several glasses, test all four drops at the same time.)
flow.say: Do the room-temperature drop first. Press a finger on the top of the straw and lift it out. Lower the tip to the middle of the glass. Let go. Start the timer. What does the red do? Write it down. Then refill the glass and wait two minutes for each next drop.
flow.kid: Fill a straw. Finger on top. Lower it to the middle. Let go. Start the timer. Watch.

ask.q: What does the hot drop do? What does the ice-cold drop do?
good: The hot one goes up.
The cold one goes down.
They go opposite ways.

flow.parent: The hot drop should rise to the top, often in about 2 to 10 seconds, then spread across the surface. The ice-cold drop should sink to the bottom, often in about 3 to 10 seconds. The warm drop is slower. These times are typical, and not a promise: glass size and how gently you let go change them. The room drop should stay about where it is, or drift down very slowly. If a drop smears everywhere, you pushed it out too fast, so let it run out slowly. Your times will be different, and that is fine. Write down what you really see. If nothing seems to happen, the drop was probably too small or too pale: use 4 drops of colour, or let go closer to the middle, and look from the side against the white paper. With 2 to 4 children, give each child their own glass and their own temperature. Everyone lets go on 'three, two, one', and you watch all the glasses side by side. One child is the timer and one writes the results. With one child and a parent, the parent can be timer and recorder.

check.q: The hot drop rises in the glass. What does that show about the hot water?
options: It is lighter than the cooler water around it
It is heavier than the cooler water around it
It is angry
check.why: Hot water takes up more room, so a spoonful of hot water is lighter than a spoonful of cool water. It is pushed up through the heavier water around it. If you thought it would be heavier, that is a common idea. The test shows the opposite.

flow.context: In this step, you test the four drops one by one and time them.

flow.do: Draw the glass with four arrows to show where each drop went. Then ask your child to say three things: what they thought (claim), what they saw (evidence), and why it happened (reasoning).
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think the hot drop and the cold drop went opposite ways?
flow.kid: Draw four arrows in the glass. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says the hot water was lighter and rose, and the cold water was heavier and sank. After they have said what they saw, you can add: hot water expands, so it is less dense, and the cooler water around it is heavier and sinks underneath it and pushes it up. Moving water that carries heat is called convection. If your results were different, for example the room drop sank, say that too. It may be because of the colour, and testing again with less colour will check.
flow.think: If the hot drop went up, where did the cooler water come from to take its place?
flow.context: This is the last step of Colour Currents. You say what you found out.

experiments.title: Dark, White and Shiny: which wrapping lets the Sun warm a tumbler most?
experiments.question: Three identical tumblers of water sit in the Sun. One is wrapped in black paper, one in white paper, and one in shiny kitchen foil. Which will warm up the most in 20 minutes? Which will warm up the least?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess which tumbler will warm the most and which will warm the least. Put the three in order. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three tumblers are the same size, hold the same amount of water (about 100 millilitres) at the same starting temperature, and each has a lid made of the same material as its wrapper. They sit side by side in the same sunlight for the same time. A fourth tumbler stays in the shade to show how much the room alone changes the water. Only the wrapping changes.

materials.item: 4 identical small glass or steel tumblers (clear glass is best)
a sheet of black paper, two sheets of thin white paper (use them double, because single thin white paper lets light through), and a piece of kitchen foil, each big enough to wrap round a tumbler
4 rubber bands
4 lids: a circle cut from the black paper, from the white paper and from the foil, and a white one for the shaded tumbler, each with a small slit for the thermometer
a thermometer that reads between 20 and 60 degrees. A school-lab thermometer is cheapest. A kitchen one also works
a jug of room-temperature water, enough for about 100 millilitres (half a glass) in each tumbler
a sunny balcony, window ledge or terrace
a book or wooden board to stand the tumblers on, so a hot floor does not warm them
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: Do not look at sunlight reflected off the foil. It can hurt your eyes. Keep the tumblers where they cannot fall or break, and do not leave small children alone on a terrace edge. Paper and glass left in the Sun can feel hot, so touch them first with the back of one finger. Glass thermometers can break: a grown-up holds them.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar for the rise in each tumbler. Write three sentences: what you thought (claim), what you saw (evidence), and why it happened (reasoning).
experiments.context: In this experiment, you wrap three tumblers of water in black, white and shiny foil, and find out which one the Sun warms most. This shows how radiation is taken in or sent back.

setup.art: Three tumblers in a row on a table, one wrapped in black paper, one in white paper and one in shiny foil, each held by a rubber band, with a fourth plain tumbler on the end.
setup.caption: 1. Wrap one tumbler in black paper, one in white paper and one in foil. Leave a fourth plain.

setup.art: A jug pouring the same amount of water into each tumbler, and a lid in the same colour as its wrapper on each one, with a thermometer slit.
setup.caption: 2. Fill each tumbler with the same amount of water. Put on the matching lids.

setup.art: A hand reading a thermometer through the slit in a foil lid on one tumbler, with a pencil and table beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Read and write down the starting temperature of each.

setup.art: Three wrapped tumblers side by side on a sunny balcony ledge, and the fourth tumbler standing in the shade behind them.
setup.caption: 4. Put the three wrapped tumblers side by side in full sun, and the fourth in the shade.

setup.art: A child reading the thermometer in the black tumbler after waiting, with the white and foil ones behind.
setup.caption: 5. After 10 minutes and again after 20 minutes, read each temperature.

flow.do: Show your child the tumblers, the paper and the foil. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the order they choose.
flow.say: The Sun will shine on three tumblers. One is wrapped in black, one in white, and one in shiny foil. Which will get warmest? Which will stay coolest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three tumblers in the Sun. Black, white and foil. Which warms most? Why?

ask.q: Which do you think will warm the least, and why?
good: The foil, because it is shiny.
The white one, because it is light.
They will all be the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write the order down. Many children expect the foil to be hottest because it looks bright. Others pick white. The result is not always what they expect.
flow.context: This is the first step of Dark, White and Shiny. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Wrap the black paper round the first tumbler and hold it with a rubber band. Wrap the white paper round the second. Wrap the foil round the third, with the shiny side out. Leave the fourth plain. Make a lid for each from the same paper or foil, with a small slit. Fill each tumbler with the same amount of water, about 100 millilitres. Put on the lids.
flow.say: Wrap each tumbler all the way round, with the shiny side of the foil facing out. Put the same amount of room-temperature water in each. Put a lid on each, made of the same paper or foil as its wrapper. Now the colour you chose covers the whole tumbler.
flow.kid: Wrap three tumblers. Fill them all the same. Put on lids of the same colour.
flow.parent: The Sun is high at midday in India, so it hits the top of a tumbler more than the sides. That is why each lid is the same colour as its wrapper. Fill each tumbler to the same mark with water from the same jug, about 100 millilitres, because a small amount of water warms by a bigger, easier-to-read number of degrees. Wrap two layers of white paper, or the light goes through it. If the foil is crumpled, smooth it out so it stays shiny. With 2 to 4 children, each child wraps and looks after one tumbler. With one child, the child wraps all of them.

check.q: Why does the fourth tumbler stay in the shade?
options: To show how much the room alone changes the water
To keep it from getting wet
Because it is the best one
check.why: A control shows what happens without the thing we are testing. If the shaded tumbler warms too, some of the rise in the others comes from the warm day, not only from the Sun.

flow.context: In this step, you wrap the tumblers and fill them with water.

flow.do: Read the temperature in each tumbler through the slit. Write the four starting temperatures in the table. Wipe the thermometer between tumblers.
flow.say: Put the thermometer through the slit and wait until the number stops changing. Write it down. Do this for all four.
flow.kid: Read the thermometer in each tumbler. Write the numbers down.

ask.q: Why do we need to know the starting temperatures?
good: So we can see how much each one went up.
Because the rise is what we compare.

flow.parent: All four should start within one degree of each other. If one is different, wait or swap a little water until they match. A lab thermometer takes about 30 seconds to settle. One thermometer is enough: use it in the same order every time. If you have no thermometer, use the back of one finger, rank the four tumblers from coolest to warmest by feel, and say that this is only a rough order.
flow.context: In this step, you take the starting temperatures.

flow.do: Put the three wrapped tumblers side by side in full sunlight, on the book, with the fourth in the shade. Wait 10 minutes. Read each temperature and write it down. Wait another 10 minutes. Read each again.
flow.say: Put them side by side in the Sun. Do not move them. After 10 minutes, take every reading. Read the thermometer in the same order each time. Then wait 10 minutes more and read each one again.
flow.kid: Put them in the Sun. Wait 10 minutes. Read each one. Wait again. Read again.

ask.q: What is the Sun doing to the black paper?
good: Warming it up.
The paper takes in the light and gets hot.

ask.q: Can you feel a difference with your hand?
good: The black one feels warmest.
The foil one is cool.

flow.parent: Use a sunny hour, between 11 in the morning and 2 in the afternoon. On a cloudy day, wait for another day. While you wait, you can do the Hands Around a Diya activity or draw the heat's journey. The numbers will be a little uneven, so look at the order more than the exact numbers. On a clear day the black tumbler often rises a few degrees more than the white one, and the foil one often rises least, but the gaps can be small, such as 1 or 2 degrees, on a hazy day. If the shaded tumbler rises as much as the others, the day was too hot for a clean test: try early morning or another day. If yours do not match, write down what you saw. A surprise is a result too. With 2 to 4 children, one reads the thermometer, one writes, one watches the clock, and one checks that nothing has been moved or has fallen into shade.
flow.context: In this step, you leave the tumblers in the Sun and read the temperatures twice.

flow.do: Work out the rise for each tumbler by taking the starting temperature from the last one. Draw a bar for each. Then ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Take the starting number from the last number. That is the rise. Draw a bar for each tumbler. Which rose most? Tell me what you thought, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Work out the rise for each one. Draw the bars. Say why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that dark, dull paper takes in more of the Sun's radiation and turns it into heat, while white paper and foil send much of it back. After they have said what they saw, explain: the Sun's heat travels as radiation, and what happens next depends on the surface it lands on. If the shaded tumbler warmed too, subtract its rise from the others to see what the Sun added.
flow.think: If the Sun's warmth reached the black paper through empty space and clear air, what did the paper do with it?
flow.context: This is the last step of Dark, White and Shiny. You say what you found out.

activities.title: Hands Around a Diya: where do you feel the warmth?

materials.item: a diya or a tea-light candle on a steel plate (two or three tea-lights together if the flame is small)
matches or a lighter, for a grown-up only
a piece of thin card or a book cover, about 15 centimetres square
a ruler
a pencil and a sheet of paper
a phone or kitchen timer with seconds

activities.safety: A grown-up lights the flame and stays beside the child all the time. Tie back long hair. No loose dupattas or sleeves. Keep curtains and paper away. Close any fan or window that makes a draught, so the flame does not lean. A child never reaches closer than 15 centimetres above the flame or closer than 5 centimetres to the side. The plate and the hot oil stay hot for a long time, so nobody touches them. Blow it out at the end.

schedule.what: Guess, feel the warmth in three places, block it with a card, and draw what you found.

activities.record: A drawing of the diya with three palms around it, and for each one a word: none, a little, or a lot. Write the seconds it took for the side palm to feel warm, with and without the card. Then write which of them the card blocked.
activities.context: In this activity, you hold a palm in different places near a flame, and block the warmth with a card. You find that the flame sends warmth in two different ways.

setup.art: A lit diya on a steel plate on a table, with a ruler laid beside it marking 10 centimetres to the side and 30 centimetres above.
setup.caption: 1. Put the diya on a plate. A grown-up lights it. Mark 10 centimetres to the side.

setup.art: A child's palm held flat at the side of the flame, 10 centimetres away, with a small smile.
setup.caption: 2. Hold your palm beside the flame, 10 centimetres away. Feel the warmth.

setup.art: A child's palm held high above the flame, 30 centimetres up, being lowered slowly with a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Hold your palm 30 centimetres above. Lower it slowly. Stop when it feels warm.

setup.art: A thin card standing upright between the flame and the side palm, with the other palm still above the flame.
setup.caption: 4. Stand a card between the flame and the side palm. Does the warmth stop?

flow.do: Ask your child to guess where the warmth is strongest: beside the flame, above it, or below it. Ask for a reason. Then ask what they think a card would do.
flow.say: A diya is a little heater. Where do you think you will feel the most warmth? Beside it, above it, or below it? Why do you think so? And what do you think a card would do?
flow.kid: Where will you feel the most warmth? Beside, above or below? Why?
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Children often say that heat goes in every direction equally. Write the guess down.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hands Around a Diya. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up lights the diya and tells your child to sit still. Hold a palm flat beside the flame, 10 centimetres away. Count to 10, or time how many seconds until it feels warm. Then hold the other palm 30 centimetres above the flame, and lower it slowly until it feels warm. Stop there.
flow.say: Hold one palm beside the flame, 10 centimetres away. Count slowly to 10. Now hold your other palm high above the flame. Lower it slowly. Stop when it feels warm. Never go lower than 15 centimetres.
flow.kid: Palm beside the flame. Count to 10. Palm above the flame. Lower it slowly. Stop when warm.

ask.q: Where did it feel warmer? What did you notice about where you stopped?
good: Above felt hotter.
I had to stay further away above.
The warmth above was stronger.

flow.parent: You should feel gentle warmth at the side and much stronger warmth above, even 20 to 25 centimetres up. If your child's palm gets too hot, tell them to move away. Do not let them touch the plate, which may be hot. A small tea-light gives only a gentle warmth at the side. If your child feels nothing at 10 centimetres, move the palm in to 7 centimetres (never nearer than 5) or use two or three tea-lights together. Two or three children can take turns, one at a time, while the others watch from a safe distance, hold the timer, and write the seconds.
flow.context: In this step, you feel the warmth beside the flame and above it.

flow.do: Stand the card on its edge between the flame and the palm at the side. Count the seconds until the warmth comes back when the card is taken away. Keep the other palm above the flame, but do not move it. Then take the card away.
flow.say: Now stand the card on its edge between the flame and your side palm. What happens to the warmth? Then check your palm above the flame. Did the card change that warmth?
flow.kid: Stand the card between the flame and your palm. Does the warmth stop? What about above?

ask.q: What did the card stop, and what did it not stop?
good: It stopped the warmth at the side.
It did not stop the warmth above.
The warmth above still came up.

flow.parent: The side warmth stops at once when the card goes up, and comes back when it goes away. The warmth above is not blocked by a card at the side. Do not explain yet. Let your child say what they think the two kinds of warmth are. Ask a second child, or the grown-up, to hold the card so the first child's hands stay still. Record the seconds in the drawing.

check.q: The card stopped the warmth at the side straight away. What does this tell you about that warmth?
options: It travels in straight lines from the flame, like light
It was carried by moving air
It was a trick
check.why: Something that can be blocked at once by a thin card travels in straight lines, like light. This is radiation. The warmth above is hot air rising from the flame, and a card at the side cannot stop it. This is convection. If you chose moving air, notice that moving air would go round a card.

flow.context: In this step, you block the warmth with a card and see which warmth it stops.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the diya and the two palms. Write one word near each: radiation or convection, with an arrow to show where the warmth travels. Ask them to explain.
flow.say: Draw the diya and your two palms. Draw an arrow to show how the warmth got to each palm. One kind went in straight lines. The other was carried upwards by hot air. Which was which?
flow.kid: Draw the flame and both hands. Draw arrows. Which kind of warmth was which?
flow.parent: Now you can say the words. Warmth in straight lines that a card can block is radiation. Warm air rising and carrying heat is convection. A flame does both at once, and also conducts heat slowly into the plate.
flow.think: Why can you feel strong warmth above the flame, but only gentle warmth beside it?
flow.context: This is the last step of Hands Around a Diya. You draw what the heat did.

activities.title: Paper Spiral: can rising air turn a snake of paper?

materials.item: a sheet of thin paper, A4 size (notebook or printer paper, not card)
scissors
a pencil
thread or thin string, 40 centimetres long
a stick or long ruler to hang the thread from
a diya or 2 to 3 tea-lights together on a steel plate, and matches for a grown-up

activities.safety: A grown-up lights the flame and holds the spiral. Keep the paper at least 15 centimetres above the flame. Never hold a spiral over a flame and walk away. Keep curtains and other paper away, and tie back long hair. If the paper starts to brown or curl, move it away at once. Blow out the flame at the end. Scissors are used by the child with a grown-up beside them.

schedule.what: Cut a spiral, hang it above a flame, and find out what makes it turn.

activities.record: A drawing of the spiral above the flame, with arrows showing where the air moves. Write how many turns in 20 seconds at each height you tried.
activities.context: In this activity, you make a paper spiral and hang it above a small flame. You find out what moves it, and where the air comes from.

setup.art: A circle drawn on thin paper with a spiral line drawn inside it, from the edge to the centre.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a circle on paper. Draw a spiral inside it, round and round to the middle.

setup.art: Scissors cutting along the spiral line to make a paper snake that hangs down in coils.
setup.caption: 2. Cut along the spiral line. Tie the thread to the middle.

setup.art: A grown-up holding the spiral on a stick, 25 centimetres above a lit diya, with the spiral beginning to turn.
setup.caption: 3. Hold the spiral on a stick 25 centimetres above the diya. Watch.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess what will happen to the spiral when it hangs above a flame, and why. Write the guess.
flow.say: We are going to hang a paper spiral above a small flame. There is no wind and nobody will blow it. What do you think will happen? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A paper spiral above a flame. What will happen? Why?
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say that it will burn, or that nothing will happen.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Paper Spiral. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Draw a circle about 12 centimetres across on the paper. Draw a spiral inside it, going round three or four times to the middle. Cut out the circle. Cut along the spiral line. Poke a small hole in the middle and tie the thread through it.
flow.say: Draw a circle about as wide as your hand. Draw a spiral inside it, round and round to the middle. Cut along the spiral line, and then tie the thread in the middle.
flow.kid: Draw a circle. Draw a spiral. Cut along it. Tie the thread.
flow.parent: Scissors are for the child to use, with help. The coils should hang down like a paper snake when you lift the spiral by the middle. Make the paper thin. Thick card is too heavy to turn.
flow.context: In this step, you make the paper spiral.

flow.do: A grown-up lights the diya or the bunched tea-lights on a plate on a table. Tie the thread to a stick. Untwist the thread and let the spiral settle. Hold it on the stick 25 centimetres above the flame, and keep it still. If it does not turn, lower it slowly to 15 centimetres, but no lower. Count how many full turns it makes in 20 seconds.
flow.say: Hold the spiral on the stick, 25 centimetres above the flame, and keep your hand still. Watch. Does it turn? Which way? Count the turns in 20 seconds.
flow.kid: Hold the spiral above the flame. Keep still. Does it turn? Count the turns.

ask.q: What is turning the spiral? Nobody is blowing it.
good: The air above the flame.
Hot air going up.
The warm air pushes on it.

ask.q: Where does new air come from to replace the air that went up?
good: From the sides.
From below, near the plate.
From the cool room.

flow.parent: The spiral turns slowly, because warm air is rising past its slanted coils. It is a slow turn, perhaps a full turn every few seconds, and one tea-light at 25 centimetres may give only a small wobble. That is why two or three tea-lights close together, thin paper and 15 to 20 centimetres work better. Never go nearer than 15 centimetres. A draught from a fan will mess up the result, so switch off any fans and close the window. If it still does not turn, check that the coils hang apart, and say honestly that the warm air was too weak. Try again with more tea-lights. With 2 to 4 children, one holds the stick with a grown-up beside them, one counts turns, one times 20 seconds, one writes. Everyone makes their own spiral first.

options: Warm air rising from the flame pushes on its slanted coils
The light from the flame pushes it
Heat travelling through the thread
check.why: The flame warms the air above it. The warm air is lighter than the air around it, so it rises, and it pushes on the slanted coils. If you chose the thread, remember that paper and thread carry heat very slowly. If you chose light, the push of light is far too small to turn paper.

flow.context: In this step, you hang the spiral above the flame and watch it turn.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the diya and the spiral, with arrows showing where the air goes. Ask where the air comes from at the bottom.
flow.say: Draw the flame and the spiral. Draw arrows for the air. The air goes up over the flame. Where does the air come from at the bottom? Draw that too.
flow.kid: Draw the flame, the spiral and the air. Where does new air come from?
flow.parent: A good drawing has air rising over the flame and cooler air flowing in from the sides along the table to take its place. That is a convection current.
flow.think: If you put the flame in a tall jar with a lid on, what would happen to the spiral?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Paper Spiral. You draw the loop of moving air.

activities.title: Draw the Heat's Journey: three ways in one kitchen picture

materials.item: a big sheet of paper
pencils or crayons in at least three colours
a steel spoon and a wooden or plastic spoon of the same length, and a steel glass or katori
hot water from the kettle, poured by a grown-up

schedule.what: Test a steel spoon and a wooden spoon in hot water, then draw a pot on a stove and show three ways the heat travels.

activities.record: A drawing of a pot of dal on a stove, with a ladle in it and a child nearby, and three coloured arrows for conduction, convection and radiation.
activities.context: In this activity, you draw a pot on a stove and show all three ways heat travels in one picture. Drawing the parts you cannot see helps you understand them.

setup.art: A large sheet of paper with a drawing of a pot of dal on a gas flame, a steel ladle in the pot, and a child standing close on the right.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the stove, the pot, the ladle in the pot, and a child standing close.

setup.art: A red arrow going up the ladle handle and a blue loop of arrows going up the middle, across the top and down the sides of the pot.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a red arrow up the ladle and a blue loop of arrows inside the dal.

setup.art: Orange wavy lines going from the flame and the hot pot sideways to the child's face.
setup.caption: 3. Draw orange wavy lines from the pot to the child's face. Name each arrow.

flow.do: First a quick test. A grown-up pours hot (not boiling) water into the steel glass. Stand the steel spoon and the wooden spoon in it, leaning on the rim. Ask your child to guess which handle will feel warm first. After 2 minutes, touch both handles with a fingertip and say which is warmer. Then ask your child to draw a stove with a pot of dal on it. Add a steel ladle in the dal. Add a child standing close. Do not add the arrows yet.
flow.say: Draw a gas stove with a pot of dal on it. Put a steel ladle in the pot. Draw a child standing near, on the right. We will add the heat arrows next.
flow.kid: Draw a stove, a pot, a ladle and a child. No arrows yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of Draw the Heat's Journey. You draw the picture first.
flow.parent: The steel handle warms noticeably in a minute or two. The wooden one stays nearly cool. This is a real measurement of how well each material conducts heat. Write which was warmer and by how much it felt (a little, a lot). Do not correct the guess before the test. If both feel the same, the spoons may be too short or the water too cool, so use more hot water. With 2 to 4 children, each child feels one spoon at a time and says what they notice.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw a red arrow up the handle of the ladle. Then ask them to draw a blue loop of arrows inside the pot of dal. Ask where the dal at the bottom goes when it is heated.
flow.say: Draw a red arrow up the ladle handle. Draw a blue loop of arrows inside the dal. Which way does the hot dal go? Where does it go when it reaches the top?
flow.kid: Draw a red arrow up the ladle. Draw a blue loop in the dal.

ask.q: Which way does the dal at the bottom go when it is hot? And then?
good: It goes up in the middle.
It spreads across the top and goes down at the sides.

flow.parent: The red arrow shows heat creeping from part to part along the steel. The blue loop is the dal rising over the flame, sinking at the sides, and coming round again.
flow.context: In this step, you draw conduction and convection.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw orange wavy lines from the pot and the flame to the child's face. Then label each of the three kinds of arrow with its name.
flow.say: Draw wavy orange lines from the flame and the hot pot to the child's face. The child feels warmth on the face, but the air between is not carrying it. Now write the name next to each kind of arrow.
flow.kid: Draw wavy lines to the face. Label all three kinds of arrows.

ask.q: Why are the lines to the face wavy and in every direction?
good: Because radiation goes out in all directions.
It is like light.

flow.parent: Radiation goes out from the flame and the hot pot in every direction, and is felt on the skin wherever it lands. The words to label with are conduction, convection and radiation.
flow.context: In this step, you draw radiation and label all three.

flow.do: Ask your child to point to one arrow and explain it. Ask what would stop each kind of heat: a lid, a wooden handle, a card between pot and face.
flow.say: Pick one arrow and explain it to me. Then tell me: how could you stop each kind of heat? A wooden handle? A lid? A card held between the pot and your face?
flow.kid: Explain one arrow. How could you stop each one?
flow.parent: A wooden handle slows conduction. A lid slows convection, because it traps the rising hot steam. A card blocks radiation straight away. Only radiation can work with no air.
flow.think: Which of the three could still work if there were no air at all?
flow.context: This is the last step of Draw the Heat's Journey. You explain what you drew.

activities.safety: A grown-up pours the hot water, and the child does not carry it. Use water that is hot but not boiling, about 60 degrees. Only the spoon handles are touched, never the water.

activities.title: Act Out the Sea Breeze: land, sea and the Sun

materials.item: an open floor space, about 3 metres by 3 metres
a blue sheet or dupatta for the sea, and a yellow or brown sheet for the land
2 to 4 people to act, including a grown-up (or soft toys, if it is just you and a parent)

schedule.what: Act out a hot afternoon and a cool night at the beach.

activities.record: A drawing of a beach in the afternoon and at night, with arrows to show which way the wind blows each time.
activities.context: In this activity, you act out why the wind blows from the sea to the land in the day and the other way at night. Acting out a loop helps you remember which way it goes.

setup.art: A floor with a blue sheet on one side as the sea and a yellow sheet on the other side as the land, and a child standing in the middle as the Sun, with arms raised.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the blue sheet as the sea and the yellow sheet as the land. One person is the Sun.

setup.art: Two children standing on the yellow land sheet rising on tiptoes with arms up, and two children walking in from the blue sea sheet along the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Afternoon: land air gets warm and rises. Sea air walks in underneath.

setup.art: The same floor at night, with the children from the sea now on tiptoe and the land children walking out along the floor.
setup.caption: 3. Night: the land cools and the sea stays warmer. The wind turns round.

flow.do: Lay out the blue sheet and the yellow sheet side by side. Choose one person as the Sun. Two people are land air on the yellow sheet. Two people are sea air on the blue sheet. Ask your child to guess which way the wind will blow in the afternoon.
flow.say: Blue is the sea, and yellow is the land. One of us is the Sun. Two of us are land air, and two are sea air. In the afternoon, the Sun shines on both. Which way will the wind blow, from the sea to the land or from the land to the sea? Why?
flow.kid: Blue is the sea. Yellow is the land. One person is the Sun. Which way will the wind blow?
flow.parent: With one child and a parent, the parent is the Sun, and the child moves soft toys as the air, one set for land and one set for sea. With 4 children, one is the Sun, one is the sea air, one is the land air, and one calls out the story and draws the arrows. Swap roles for the night round. Do not correct the guess yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of Act Out the Sea Breeze. You guess before you act.

flow.do: The Sun shines on the yellow land first and strongest. The land air warms up and rises on tiptoe with arms up. The sea air walks over along the floor to fill the space. Then the land air spreads across the top and walks back out over the sea, and sinks down. Do the loop twice.
flow.say: The Sun warms the land more than the sea. Land air, warm up and rise on tiptoe. Sea air, walk in along the floor to take the empty place. Rising air, spread over the top and sink down over the sea. Go round again.
flow.kid: Land air warms up and rises on tiptoe. Sea air walks in along the floor.

ask.q: Which way did the wind blow along the floor?
good: From the sea to the land.
Towards the warm land.

ask.q: Why does the sea air move?
good: Because the warm air went up and left a space.
The cool air pushes in under the warm air.

flow.parent: The wind at the floor goes from sea to land. The wind at the top goes the other way. The two together make one loop.
flow.context: In this step, you act out the sea breeze in the afternoon.

flow.do: Now it is night. The Sun goes away. The land cools quickly and the sea stays warmer. Swap the parts. The sea air warms and rises on tiptoe. The land air walks out along the floor to fill the space. Do the loop twice.
flow.say: Night comes, and the Sun is gone. The land cools quickly, but the sea stays warm. Now the sea air is the warm one. Sea air, rise on tiptoe. Land air, walk out along the floor to take its place.
flow.kid: Night comes. The sea is warmer now. Sea air rises. Land air walks out.

ask.q: Which way does the wind blow along the floor now?
good: From the land to the sea.
Away from the land.

ask.q: Why did it turn round?
good: Because the land is cooler than the sea at night.
The warm part changed.

flow.parent: The night land breeze is usually gentler than the afternoon sea breeze. Fishing boats leave a beach early in the morning on the land breeze, and come home on the sea breeze.
flow.context: In this step, you act out the land breeze at night.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the beach at noon and at midnight, with arrows for the wind. Ask what would happen to the sea breeze on a cloudy day, when the Sun is hidden.
flow.say: Draw the beach in the afternoon and at night. Use arrows for the wind. Now think about a cloudy day, when the land stays cool. What will the sea breeze do?
flow.kid: Draw the beach by day and by night. Arrows for the wind.
flow.parent: On a cloudy day, the land does not warm up as much, so the sea breeze is weak or comes late. That is why a cloudy afternoon on the coast can feel still. To see the real reason, try this on a sunny day: put one katori of dry sand or soil and one katori of water of the same amount on a window ledge in the Sun for 15 minutes. Touch each with the back of a finger. The sand is warmer to touch than the water. This is why the land warms faster than the sea.
flow.think: Which is warmer in the evening, a rock on the beach or a tub of sea water? Why does that matter for the wind?
flow.context: This is the last step of Act Out the Sea Breeze. You draw both winds.

projects.title: Foil Sun Oven: melt a piece of chocolate with sunlight alone

materials.item: a cardboard box with a lid, such as a shoebox or a sweet box, about 25 centimetres long
kitchen aluminium foil
black paper or a black cloth to line the base
clear cling film or a clear plastic bag, enough to cover the opening
tape and scissors
a pencil or stick to prop up the flap
2 squares of chocolate (or 2 slices of cheese), each on a small piece of black paper. One goes in the oven and one stays outside as a comparison
a sunny balcony or terrace
optional: a thermometer to hang inside the oven

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the lid. Never look at the Sun, or at sunlight bouncing off the foil. Keep the oven where it cannot fall. The inside can get hot, so use a spoon or tongs to take out the chocolate. Treat the chocolate as a science sample and do not eat it: it has touched foil and paper, and some chocolate has nuts or milk that some children cannot eat. Wipe up melted chocolate at once.

schedule.what: Build the oven, aim it at the Sun, and watch the chocolate.

projects.record: Write the time you put both pieces of chocolate in, and the time each began to soften and to melt. Draw the oven and the path of the sunlight into it.
projects.context: In this project, you build a simple oven that uses sunlight alone, and test how long it takes to melt chocolate. It uses radiation that is reflected and then absorbed, and trapped warm air.

setup.art: A cardboard box on a table with a flap cut in its lid on three sides, and a child lining the inside of the flap with shiny foil.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts a flap in the lid. Line the inside of the flap with foil.

setup.art: The inside of the box lined with black paper on the base and foil on the walls, with a square of chocolate in the middle.
setup.caption: 2. Line the base with black paper, and the walls with foil. Put the chocolate on black paper.

setup.art: A sheet of clear cling film taped over the opening of the box under the flap, with the flap propped open at an angle by a pencil.
setup.caption: 3. Cover the opening with cling film. Prop the flap open at an angle.

setup.art: The box on a sunny balcony ledge with the foil flap angled so that sunlight bounces into the box, and a shadow of the box on the ground.
setup.caption: 4. Turn the oven to face the Sun. Check that the sunlight bounces into the box.

flow.do: Show your child the materials. Ask them to guess if the oven will melt chocolate, and what each part of the oven is for. Write down their ideas.
flow.say: We are going to make an oven that uses only the Sun. There is no fire and no electricity. Do you think it will melt chocolate? What do you think the foil is for? And the black paper? Why?
flow.kid: An oven that uses only the Sun. Will it melt chocolate? What is the foil for?
flow.parent: Do not correct the ideas. After the test, you can look back at them. Good ideas are that the foil sends the light in and the black paper takes it in.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Foil Sun Oven. You guess before you build.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts a flap in the lid, on three sides, so it folds up like a window. Line the inside of the flap with foil, shiny side out. Line the walls with foil and the base with black paper. Tape clear cling film over the opening under the flap. Prop the flap with a pencil at an angle.
flow.say: A grown-up cuts the lid, leaving a flap that folds up. Cover the inside of the flap with shiny foil. Line the walls with foil and the base with black paper. Stretch cling film over the opening and tape it down. Prop the flap open so it bounces sunlight into the box.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts a flap in the lid. Line the flap and walls with foil. Line the base with black paper.
flow.parent: The flap should lean back at about 100 to 120 degrees so that it catches the Sun and bounces it into the box. Smooth the foil, because crumples scatter the light. Make the cling film tight and sealed, so warm air stays inside.

check.q: Why is the base lined with black paper, and the walls with foil?
options: Black takes in the light and gets hot, and foil sends light towards it
Black is prettier
Foil makes the box strong
check.why: Dark, dull surfaces absorb radiation and turn it into heat. Shiny foil reflects radiation, so the walls and flap bounce more sunlight onto the black base. If you chose black being prettier, think about what a black cloth does in the Sun.

flow.context: In this step, you build the oven.

flow.do: Put one square of chocolate on a bit of black paper in the middle of the box. Put the second square on black paper in the Sun right beside the oven, as a comparison. Put the oven in full sun on a balcony or terrace. Turn it so that the flap bounces light onto the chocolate. Check every 10 minutes. Write down when each piece of chocolate gets soft, and when it melts.
flow.say: Put the chocolate in the middle of the base. Turn the oven to face the Sun. Check every ten minutes. Turn the oven again if the Sun has moved. When does the chocolate go soft? When does it melt?
flow.kid: Put the chocolate in. Face the Sun. Check every 10 minutes. Turn the oven if the Sun moves.

ask.q: What is the Sun doing to the black paper under the chocolate?
good: Warming it up.
The paper takes in the light and gets hot.

ask.q: Why does the cling film help?
good: It traps the warm air.
The warm air cannot get out.

flow.parent: On a bright day, between 11 and 2, chocolate in the oven often goes soft in about 20 to 30 minutes and melts in about 30 to 60 minutes, if the day is clear. Times are typical, not a promise. The piece outside the oven should stay firm much longer, and that difference is your evidence. On a cloudy or hazy day, or in winter, it may not melt at all. If so, try a second day. If it is very hot, put a spoon under the chocolate to protect the paper. Never leave the oven out in the Sun and walk away. If nothing happens, check for gaps in the cling film, crumpled foil, or a flap that is not aimed at the Sun, and turn the oven every 10 minutes. With 2 to 4 children, one watches the clock, one turns the oven, one writes the times, and one looks at the outside chocolate. With one child, the child does all of these.

check.q: The warm air inside the oven cannot escape because of the cling film. Which way of moving heat does the film stop?
options: Convection, because it stops hot air from rising out
Radiation, because light cannot go through it
Conduction, because it is cold
check.why: Hot air rises and carries heat away by convection. The clear film lets sunlight in but stops the hot air from leaving. If you chose radiation, remember that clear film lets sunlight through.

flow.context: In this step, you aim the oven and wait for the chocolate to melt.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the oven with the sunlight arrows going in and bouncing. Ask which two ideas from this unit made the oven work. Ask how they could make it hotter.
flow.say: Draw your oven and the sunlight. Which two ideas from this unit made the oven work? How could we make it hotter next time?
flow.kid: Draw the oven and the sunlight. What made it work? How can we make it hotter?
flow.parent: Good answers are reflecting radiation onto a dark surface, and trapping warm air so convection cannot take it away. To make it hotter, use a bigger reflector, a better seal, or a black pot with a lid.
flow.think: Why do real solar cookers in India often have a black pot and a curved mirror?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Foil Sun Oven. You think about what made it work.

challenges.title: Cool Roof: keep a shoebox house coolest in the Sun
challenges.problem: You have three identical shoebox houses, and one hot hour of sunlight. Cover the roof of each with something different to keep the inside as cool as possible. Which roof keeps the box coolest, and by how much?
constraints: Each box has the same size roof and walls.
You can only change the covering on the roof.
Each roof covering must be made from things you already have at home.
The boxes must sit side by side in the Sun for the same 30 minutes.
Read each thermometer inside the box at the start and at the end.
materials: black paper, white paper and kitchen foil
general: A white roof, to reflect as much sunlight as possible.
A shiny foil roof with the shiny side out.
A dark roof, as a test to compare with the other two.
creative: A foil roof held 3 centimetres above the box on little cardboard legs, so air can flow between.
A white roof with a wet cloth on top, to see if water helps too.
A roof with a high gap at the top of the walls, so hot air can escape, like the ventilators in an old courtyard house.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your plan. Build it, and test it in the Sun. Change one thing, such as the air gap above the roof, and test again. Which roof kept the inside coolest? Why do you think it did?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about radiation and cool roofs. You make the best shoebox roof you can for a hot day.

setup.art: Three identical shoeboxes in a row, one with a black paper roof, one with a white paper roof and one with a shiny foil roof.
setup.caption: 1. Cover the roof of each box with something different.

setup.art: A thermometer inside each box, with the cord or stem going out through a small hole in the side.
setup.caption: 2. Put a thermometer inside each box, and read the starting temperatures.

setup.art: The three boxes side by side in full sun on a balcony ledge, and a child checking a clock.
setup.caption: 3. Put the boxes side by side in the Sun for 30 minutes. Read the thermometers.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child to sketch three roof designs, and to guess which one will keep the box coolest.
flow.say: You have three shoebox houses and a hot hour of sunlight. How could you cover the roofs to keep the inside cool? Draw three ideas. Which do you think will work best, and why?
flow.kid: Three boxes. Three roofs. Draw some ideas. Which will be coolest?

ask.q: What would make a roof stay cooler?
good: Something white.
Something shiny.
A gap for air to move.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Cool Roof challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Build the three boxes. Cover each roof with a different covering. Cut a small hole in the side of each box to put the thermometer in. Read the starting temperatures and write them down.
flow.say: Cover each roof with something different. Make a small hole in the side of each box for the thermometer. Read the starting temperatures. Write them down.
flow.kid: Cover each roof. Put a thermometer in each box. Write the starting numbers.
flow.parent: Seal the gaps at the lid with tape so air cannot leak. All three boxes must start at about the same temperature. If they do not, wait a little in the shade.
flow.context: In this step, you build the boxes and take the starting temperatures.

flow.do: Put the three boxes side by side in full Sun for 30 minutes. Read the thermometers after 15 minutes and after 30 minutes. Write the numbers down. Then work out how much each box warmed.
flow.say: Put them side by side in the Sun. Read the thermometers after 15 minutes. Read them again after 30 minutes. How much did each one warm? Which roof was best?
flow.kid: Put the boxes in the Sun. Read the thermometers. Which stayed coolest?

ask.q: Why does the white or shiny roof keep the box cooler?
good: It sends the Sun's heat back.
It does not take in so much sunlight.

flow.parent: On a bright day, the black-roof box usually warms several degrees more than the white or foil one. If the difference is small, the sun may be weak or the boxes may have gaps. Try again on another day.
flow.context: In this step, you test the roofs in the Sun.

flow.do: Change one thing about your best design, such as adding an air gap above the roof. Test it again for 15 minutes. Write down both results and say which is better.
flow.say: Change just one thing. Add a gap of air above the roof, or add a high hole in the wall. Test it again. Is it cooler or warmer?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again. Better or worse?
flow.parent: Change only one thing at a time, or you will not know which change worked. The air gap works because hot air under the roof rises out instead of heating the box by conduction.
flow.think: In a real city, who could paint a roof white, and who might not be able to?
flow.context: In this step, you improve the design and test again.

challenges.title: Cool the Jug Fast: where should the ice go?
challenges.problem: You have two jugs of warm water and four ice cubes. Cool the water in a jug as much as you can in 10 minutes, without putting ice into the water. Where should the ice go: at the top or at the bottom?
constraints: The ice stays in a zip bag or sealed bag, and does not touch the water.
You use the same number of ice cubes in each jug.
You read the temperature near the top of the water at the start and after 10 minutes.
materials: 2 tall identical jugs or glasses, each with 300 millilitres of bath-warm water
a steel spoon or a coin to weigh down one bag
general: Put the bag of ice on top of the water, hanging from the rim.
Wrap the jug with a cold wet cloth.
Put the ice in the middle of the jug.
creative: Hang a sealed bottle of ice into the water from the top, so the cold water sinks past it all the way down.
Freeze a plastic bottle of water and stand it in the jug.
Put a thin sheet of foil between the ice and the room, so it takes in less heat from the air.
challenges.your_turn: Make a plan. Test it against a jug with the ice weighed down at the bottom. Which jug had the coolest water at the top after 10 minutes? Why do you think so?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about convection. You find out where cold should go to cool a drink fastest.

setup.art: Two identical jugs of warm water side by side, one with a bag of ice held at the top and one with a bag of ice weighed down at the bottom with a steel spoon.
setup.caption: 1. Hang one bag of ice at the top. Weigh down the other bag at the bottom.

setup.art: A thermometer in the top of each jug of water, and a timer showing 10 minutes.
setup.caption: 2. Read the starting temperatures at the top of both jugs.

setup.art: Two jugs side by side, with arrows showing cold water sinking from the top ice all the way down, and a layer of cold water stuck at the bottom of the other.
setup.caption: 3. After 10 minutes, read the temperature at the top of both jugs.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child to guess which jug will be cooler at the top after 10 minutes. Is it the jug with ice on top, or ice at the bottom? Ask why.
flow.say: You have two jugs of warm water and two bags of ice. Where should the ice go to cool the water fastest, at the top or at the bottom? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two jugs. Ice at the top, or ice at the bottom? Which cools faster? Why?

ask.q: What do you think cold water does in a jug?
good: It sinks.
It stays where it is.
It spreads out.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children guess that the ice at the bottom will do better because the cold is closer to everything.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Cool the Jug challenge. You guess.

flow.do: Fill each jug with 300 millilitres of bath-warm water. Read the temperature near the top of each and write it down. Put a bag of two ice cubes at the top of the first jug. Put a bag of two ice cubes, weighed down with a spoon, at the bottom of the second.
flow.say: Fill two jugs with bath-warm water. Check the temperature at the top of each. Hang an ice bag at the top of one jug. Weigh down the other ice bag at the bottom of the second jug. Start the timer.
flow.kid: Fill both jugs. Read the temperatures. Ice at the top of one. Ice at the bottom of the other.
flow.parent: Bath-warm water is about 40 degrees and safe to touch. Both jugs should start within one degree of each other. The bag at the bottom must be sealed and held down firmly, or it will float up. Do not stir.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the two jugs.

flow.do: After 10 minutes, read the temperature near the top of each jug. Then dip a clean finger into the top and the bottom of each jug, and feel the difference. Write down what you find.
flow.say: After ten minutes, read the temperature at the top of each jug. Then touch the water at the top and at the bottom. Which jug is cooler at the top? What does the bottom of the other feel like?
flow.kid: Read the top of each jug. Touch the top and the bottom. What do you feel?

ask.q: In which jug did the cold water spread through the whole jug, and why?
good: The one with the ice at the top.
Cold water sinks, so it moved through the jug.

ask.q: In which jug did the cold stay in one layer?
good: The one with the ice at the bottom.
The cold water stayed down there.

flow.parent: The jug with the ice at the top should be clearly cooler at the top. In the jug with the ice at the bottom, the bottom may feel cold while the top is still warm, because cold water is heavier and stays down there. The results can be small if the ice is small, so use the temperatures and what your finger feels.
flow.context: In this step, you read the temperatures and feel the layers.

flow.do: Ask your child which jug was cooler at the top. Ask them to explain why, using the words warm, cool, light and heavy. Then ask how they would cool a pot of soup quickly.
flow.say: Which jug was cooler at the top? Explain why. Use the words warm, cool, light and heavy. Now tell me how you would cool a hot pot of soup quickly.
flow.kid: Which jug was cooler at the top? Why? How would you cool soup fast?
flow.parent: Cold at the top works because the cold water sinks and sets up a loop that moves all the water past the ice. Heat at the bottom works for the same reason. Put the heat low and the cold high. To cool soup quickly, stand the pot in a bowl of cold water with ice, or stir it.
flow.think: Where should the heater go in a pot of water, and where should the ice go in a jug?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Cool the Jug challenge. You explain what you found.
