quiz.p: Heat reaches your face from a bonfire across a gap of cold air. Which way is it travelling?
opts: Radiation
Conduction
Convection
quiz.why: The warmth crosses the air in straight lines without the air carrying it. That is radiation.

quiz.p: A hot-air balloon rises. What makes the hot air in it rise?
opts: It is less dense than the cooler air around it
Heat has a lifting force
The balloon's cloth pulls it up
quiz.why: Heated air expands, so each spoonful is lighter than the cooler air outside. The heavier cool air pushes it up.

quiz.p: In a convection current in a pot of water, where does the water sink?
opts: Where it has cooled, away from the flame
Directly over the flame
It never sinks
quiz.why: Water rises over the flame and spreads at the top, where it cools. Cooler water is heavier and sinks at the sides.

quiz.p: At night on a beach, the land cools below the sea's temperature. Which way does the wind blow?
opts: From the land towards the sea
From the sea towards the land
It stops blowing
quiz.why: Now the sea is the warmer place, so air rises over the sea and cooler land air flows out to take its place.

quiz.p: Which way of moving heat needs nothing at all to carry it?
opts: Radiation
Conduction
Convection
quiz.why: Radiation travels as waves that can cross empty space. Conduction needs touching, and convection needs a fluid.

quiz.p: A city paints its rooftops white. How does this keep the rooms below cooler?
opts: The white paint reflects much of the Sun's radiation
The white paint makes heat disappear
The white paint cools the air
quiz.why: Light surfaces send most sunlight back, so less of it is turned into heat in the roof.

quiz.p: Heat can only ever travel upwards.
quiz.why: False. Hot fluids rise, but conduction and radiation carry heat in every direction.

quiz.p: You test hot and cold drops of coloured water in a glass. Why must the water in the glass be still first?
opts: So that stirring is not mistaken for an effect of temperature
So the water is clear
So the drops are the same size
quiz.why: A fair test changes only one thing. If the glass water is swirling, the swirls could move the drop and hide what the temperature does.

quiz.p: Milk in a pan on a stove: the pan's base is heated, and then the whole milk warms up. Which ways is the heat travelling?
opts: Conduction through the pan, then convection in the milk
Radiation only
Conduction only
quiz.why: Heat passes through the pan by conduction, and the warm milk rising and cool milk sinking spread it by convection.

quiz.p: You open the fridge on a hot day. Which of these describes what is happening best?
opts: Heat flows in, and heavy cool air spills out along the floor
Cold flows out of the fridge
The fridge makes the room colder by itself
quiz.why: Heat always goes from warm to cool, so it flows into the fridge. The cool air is heavy, so it spills low.

quiz.p: You keep one tumbler in the shade during a Sun test. What is it for?
opts: It shows how much the warm day alone changes the water
It is the best tumbler
It protects the others from the Sun
quiz.why: A control shows what happens without the thing being tested. The extra warming in the sunny tumblers is then due to the Sun.

quiz.p: A card held between a flame and your palm stops the warmth at once. What does that tell you about the warmth?
opts: It travels in straight lines, like light
It was carried by moving air
It travels through the card
quiz.why: Only something that moves in straight lines, like light, can be blocked at once by a thin card. This is radiation. Moving air would flow round the card.

quiz.p: A woollen shawl keeps you warm. Which idea explains it best?
opts: It traps still air, which carries heat very slowly
Wool makes heat
Wool is hotter than air
quiz.why: Air that cannot move cannot carry heat by convection, and it is a poor conductor. The wool holds air still next to your skin.

items.p: A steel ladle stands in a pot of hot sambar, and its handle slowly warms. Which way is the heat travelling up the handle?
opts: Conduction
Convection
Radiation
items.why: The heat passes from each tiny part of the steel to the part touching it. That is conduction. Convection needs a liquid or gas that moves, and radiation needs no touching at all.

items.p: Why does a drop of hot water rise through cooler water?
opts: It is lighter than the cooler water around it
Heat itself is lighter than water
The cooler water pulls it up
items.why: Hot water expands and is less dense, so the heavier cool water around it sinks underneath and pushes it up. Heat is not a thing that has weight, and the cool water pushes, not pulls.

items.p: Heat always travels upwards.
items.why: False. Hot liquids and gases rise, but heat in a solid spoon travels in every direction, and radiation goes out in every direction at once.

items.p: The Sun's heat crosses empty space by ____.
items.why: Empty space has nothing to touch or to flow, so only radiation can carry the Sun's heat across it.

items.p: Match each way of moving heat to what it does.
pairs: heat passes from part to touching part
heat is carried by a moving liquid or gas
heat travels as invisible light-like waves
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Conduction needs touching. Convection needs a fluid that can flow. Radiation needs nothing.

items.p: Sort each thing by what it does to sunlight.
items.a: as given
items.why: Dark, dull things take in most of the light and turn it into heat. White and shiny things send most of it back.

items.p: Put the steps of a convection current in order, starting with the first.
items: At the top it spreads out and cools
Water near the flame is warmed
The water flows back along the bottom towards the flame
The cooled water sinks at the sides
a: Water near the flame is warmed
At the top it spreads out and cools
The cooled water sinks at the sides
The water flows back along the bottom towards the flame
items.why: The loop starts with warming. The warm water rises, cools at the top, sinks at the sides and comes back to the flame to be warmed again.

items.p: On a hot afternoon, a cool wind blows from the sea onto the beach. Why?
opts: Air rises over the warm land, and cooler sea air flows in to take its place
The sea is hotter than the land in the daytime
The Moon pulls the air towards the beach
items.why: The land warms faster than the sea. The air over it rises, and cooler air from over the sea slides in underneath.

items.p: In a made-up test, a tumbler in black paper warmed from 28 to 38 degrees in the Sun. A tumbler in white paper warmed from 28 to 31 degrees. How many more degrees did the black one rise than the white one?
items.why: The black tumbler rose 38 minus 28, which is 10 degrees. The white rose 31 minus 28, which is 3 degrees. 10 minus 3 is 7. So the black one rose 7 degrees more.

items.p: Why can the Sun's heat reach the Earth, when there is empty space in between?
opts: Radiation can cross empty space
Air in space carries the heat
Conduction works through empty space
items.why: Radiation is waves of light that need nothing to travel through. There is almost no air in space, so convection and conduction cannot work there.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Warmth of a bonfire on your face, sunlight on a terrace, a lamp warming your cheek, a hot tumbler burning your fingers.
items.a: The hot tumbler
items.why: The tumbler passes heat by conduction, because it touches your fingers. The other three are radiation, which crosses a gap without touching.

items.p: Many old single-door fridges have the freezer box at the top. Explain why this works well.
items.a: The freezer cools the air next to it. Cold air is heavier than warm air, so it sinks and cools the food below. If the freezer were at the bottom, the cold air would stay down there.
items.why: A strong answer says that cooled air sinks, so the cold spreads downwards, and that this is a convection current.

items.p: Draw a pot of water on a flame. Draw arrows to show a convection current inside it.
items.a: A pot over a flame. Arrows go up in the middle, across the top, down at the sides and back along the bottom towards the flame.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a full loop, with the water rising over the flame and sinking at the sides.

items.p: Label this picture of a pot of dal on a stove: where conduction happens, where convection happens, and where radiation reaches the child.
items.a: Conduction is along the steel ladle handle or through the base of the pot. Convection is the loop of dal inside the pot. Radiation is the warmth reaching the child's face from the side.
items.why: Conduction needs touching, convection needs a moving fluid, and radiation travels in straight lines through the air.
items.art: A pot of dal on a gas stove with a steel ladle in it and a child standing on the right, with three blank label lines.

items.p: A white roof reflects more of the Sun's radiation than a black roof.
items.why: True. White surfaces send most of the light back. Dark surfaces take it in and turn it into heat.

items.p: Zoya says: 'When I open the fridge, the cold comes out.' Say what is really happening.
items.a: Heat from the warm kitchen air goes into the fridge, and the cool, heavy air from inside spills out along the floor. There is no cold stuff. Cold is just less heat.
items.why: A strong answer says that heat moves from warm to cool, and that cool air sinks because it is heavy.

items.p: A silver vacuum flask keeps tea hot for hours. What does the silver coating do?
opts: It reflects heat radiation back into the tea
It makes the tea heavier
It makes the flask magic
items.why: Silver reflects radiation, so heat from the tea is sent back. The vacuum between the walls stops conduction and convection.

items.p: A spoonful of air at 27 degrees is warmed to 57 degrees. What happens to it?
opts: It expands and becomes lighter
It shrinks and becomes heavier
It stays exactly the same
items.why: Warm air takes up more room, so the same amount of air is spread out and each spoonful is lighter. This is why warm air rises through cooler air.

items.p: Black kite birds circle higher without flapping over a hot road. What lifts them?
opts: Warm air rising from the hot road
The pull of the Sun
Their feathers make their own lift
items.why: The hot road warms the air above it, and the warm air rises in a column called a thermal. The birds ride it upwards.

items.p: When you open a window in winter, cold flows into the room.
items.why: False. There is no cold stuff. Heat flows out of the warm room to the cold outside, and the cold air that comes in is just air with less heat in it.

items.p: A surface that is good at taking in radiation is also good at ____ it out.
items.why: A black pot takes in heat well, and it also gives out heat well. That is why a black pot cools quickly once it leaves the stove.

items.p: After 30 minutes in the Sun, which tumbler usually warms most? Put these in order from warmest to coolest.
items.why: Black takes in most of the radiation. White sends back much of it. Shiny foil sends back almost all of it. The exact numbers depend on the day, but the order is usually this.

items.p: Sort each example by the main way the heat travels.
items: a steel spoon warming in hot dal
smoke curling up from an agarbatti
warmth from the Sun on your arm
a sea breeze in the afternoon
an iron tawa handle getting hot
warmth from a glowing heater to your hand
items.a: as given
items.why: Touching along a solid is conduction. A moving fluid carrying heat is convection. Warmth that crosses a gap in straight lines is radiation.

items.p: Match each wind or flow to what causes it.
pairs: land warmer than the sea in the daytime
land cooler than the sea at night
warm air rising from hot ground
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each one is a loop of warm fluid rising and cooler fluid sinking. What changes is where the warmth comes from.

items.p: A steel plate feels colder than a wooden board that has been in the same room all day. Why?
opts: Steel carries heat away from your hand faster
The steel is at a lower temperature
Wood makes its own heat
items.why: Both are at room temperature. Your skin feels the speed at which heat leaves it, and steel is a better conductor than wood.

items.p: The Moon's light takes about 1 second to reach us. The Sun's radiation takes about 500 seconds. How many times as long does the Sun's take?
items.why: 500 divided by 1 is 500. So the Sun's radiation takes about 500 times as long to reach us.

items.p: A lid on a pot of dal helps keep it hot. Say which way of moving heat the lid slows down most, and how.
items.a: The lid slows convection. Hot steam and hot air cannot rise away from the dal. The dal also loses less heat by radiation upwards.
items.why: A strong answer says that the lid traps the rising warm air and steam, so the heat stays in the pot.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Sea breeze, a thermal, boiling water, sunbathing.
items.a: Sunbathing
items.why: The first three are convection, with warm fluid rising and cool fluid sinking. Sunbathing warms your skin by radiation.

items.p: Dev and Anjali are talking about the freezer.

views.says: Cold flows out of the freezer when you open it.
There is no cold stuff. Heat flows in, and the heavy cool air spills out.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Describe a way to test it, such as a thermometer near the floor and one at the top. Then say what Dev has partly right.
items.a: Anjali is right that heat flows into the cold fridge. Dev is partly right that cool air really does spill out and feels cold. A thermometer near the floor in front of the open door would show the cool air spreading low.
items.why: A strong answer picks a side, gives a test, and says fairly that the cool air does move.

items.p: Draw an old house on a hot day. Show where cool air comes in, where hot air goes out, and which way each one moves.
items.a: A house with a low door or window open on the shaded side and a high ventilator. Arrows show cool air coming in low and moving along the floor, and hot air rising and leaving through the high ventilator.
items.why: A strong drawing shows one opening low and one high, and a loop of air through the room.

items.p: Label this picture of the Sun and the Earth: the Sun, the Earth, the empty space, and the way the heat travels.
items.a: The Sun is on the left. The Earth is on the right. The empty space is the gap in between with no air. The heat travels as radiation, shown with wavy arrows.
items.why: The Sun's heat crosses about 150 million kilometres of nearly empty space as radiation.
items.art: The Sun on the left, the Earth on the right, a wide dark gap between them with wavy lines, and four blank label lines.

items.p: Many people in hot places wear loose, light-coloured cotton. Why does this help?
opts: Light colours reflect more sunlight, and loose cloth lets air move over the skin
White cloth is cold
Cotton gives out heat
items.why: Light colours send back more of the Sun's radiation. Loose cloth lets warm air next to the skin escape and cooler air flow in.

items.p: The Sun's heat reaches us by warming all the air between the Sun and the Earth.
items.why: False. Radiation passes through clear air and empty space without warming them much. It warms the ground and our skin.

items.p: Pick something in your home where heat travels in two ways at once. Name both ways and say where each one happens.
items.a: For example, in a pot of milk on a stove, conduction passes heat through the base, and convection stirs it through the milk.
items.why: A strong answer names two different ways and points to the exact place each one happens.

items.p: A pond cools in winter. Water is heaviest at 4 degrees, and lighter just above 0 degrees. What follows?
opts: The coldest water stays at the top, so the pond freezes from the top down
The coldest water sinks to the bottom, so the pond freezes from the bottom up
The pond never freezes
items.why: Below 4 degrees, water becomes lighter as it cools. The coldest water stays on top and freezes first, and fish can survive in the 4 degree water below.

items.p: On the space station, fans must keep the air moving all the time. Why?
opts: Warm and used air does not rise in weightlessness, so breath would collect around the face
The fans are there for decoration
The station is too cold
items.why: Rising air needs gravity to pull the heavier air down. Without it, there is no natural convection, and the air around an astronaut's face would go stale.

items.p: Explain why a sea breeze is weak or late on a cloudy afternoon.
items.a: Clouds block sunlight, so the land does not warm much. Then the air over the land does not rise as strongly, and not much cooler sea air is pulled in.
items.why: A strong answer links the cloud to a cooler land, and a cooler land to a weaker rise and a weaker pull.

items.p: A black pot and a shiny pot of the same size are filled with the same hot water and left to cool. Which cools faster by radiation, and why?
opts: The black pot, because dark surfaces are good at giving out radiation
The shiny pot, because it is shiny
They cool at exactly the same rate
items.why: A surface that takes in radiation well also gives it out well. A shiny surface is poor at both, so it holds its heat longer.

items.p: When a warm fluid cools at the top of a loop, it becomes ____ and sinks.
items.why: Cooling makes the fluid shrink a little, so each spoonful is heavier. Heavier fluid sinks.

items.p: In a vacuum flask, the empty gap between the walls stops both conduction and convection.
items.why: True. With nothing in the gap, there is nothing to touch and nothing to flow. Only radiation can cross, which the silver coating reflects.

items.p: A school classroom in Madurai gets very hot by 2 in the afternoon. Three people have different ideas.

views.says: Open the high windows and the low doors, so hot air can leave and cooler air can come in.
Paint the tin roof white, so it reflects the Sun.
Buy air coolers for every room.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing another person has right, and who might not be able to afford each idea.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and uses a fact, such as white roofs reflecting radiation or high and low openings making a loop of air. It also admits a fair point from another idea, such as cost or electricity.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Each choice uses a real idea, and a strong answer is fair about cost and who can afford what.

items.p: In a made-up test, the top of the water in a jug with the ice at the top fell by 12 degrees. In a jug with the ice at the bottom, the top fell by 3 degrees. How many times as far did the first fall?
items.why: 12 divided by 3 is 4. So the top of the first jug fell 4 times as far.

items.p: Match each thing to the idea that explains it.
pairs: A candle flame is a ball in space
A foil lid on a tumbler
hot air rises and draws fresh air in
cool air comes in low and hot air leaves high
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each one uses rising warm fluid, sinking cool fluid, or reflected radiation in a different place.

items.p: Put in order how the Sun's heat warms a tumbler of water in a black wrapping.
items: The water warms up and stirs in loops
The black paper takes it in and warms up
The glass passes the heat to the water
a: The black paper takes it in and warms up
The glass passes the heat to the water
The water warms up and stirs in loops
items.why: The journey uses all three ways. Radiation crosses space and lands on the paper. Conduction carries heat through the glass. Convection stirs the water.

items.p: Which of these is not a real thing? A thermal, a caloric fluid, infrared light, a convection current.
items.a: A caloric fluid
items.why: A caloric fluid was an idea from the 1700s, that heat is a weightless liquid. It was shown to be wrong. The other three are real.

items.p: A black kite rises without flapping. Follow the energy back as far as you can. Start with the bird.
items.a: The bird is lifted by rising air. The air is warmed by the hot ground. The ground is warmed by the Sun's radiation. The Sun's energy comes from the nuclear reactions in its core.
items.why: A strong answer follows the chain: bird, rising air, warm ground, sunlight, and the Sun itself.

items.p: Draw a rooftop solar water heater with a tank on top and a black panel below it. Show where the water goes as it warms.
items.a: A black panel at the bottom with water inside, a tank above it. Arrows show warm water rising from the panel into the tank, and cool water sinking from the tank back into the panel.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a loop, with the warm water rising to the top of the tank and cool water coming down.

items.p: Label this picture of a sea breeze: the warm land, the cool sea, the rising air, and the wind along the ground.
items.a: The warm land is on the right. The cool sea is on the left. The rising air is above the land. The wind along the ground blows from the sea to the land.
items.why: The land warms faster, so air rises over it, and cooler sea air flows in below.
items.art: A beach scene with a sea on the left and land on the right, a loop of arrows, and four blank label lines.

items.p: In 1856, Eunice Foote found that a jar of carbon dioxide warmed more in sunlight than a jar of ordinary air. What does this suggest?
opts: Carbon dioxide takes in more of the Sun's heat radiation than ordinary air does
Carbon dioxide is a colder gas
The air in the other jar was too small
items.why: Her jars were otherwise the same. The difference suggests that the gas inside changed how much heat was held. This is an early clue to the greenhouse effect.

items.p: You want to check whether a white roof really keeps a room cooler than a dark roof. Say what you would keep the same, what you would change, and what you would measure.
items.a: Keep the same: the size of the rooms, the walls, and the time in the Sun. Change: the colour of the roof. Measure: the temperature inside the rooms, at the start and after the same time.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing, keeps the rest the same, and measures with a thermometer.

open_questions.q: Why is the Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona, hotter than the Sun's surface by hundreds of times?
open_questions.why_open: Heat normally flows from hot to cool, so the corona should be cooler than the surface it sits on. Scientists have several ideas about waves and tiny flares, but none is settled.

open_questions.q: How much do the slow currents in the Earth's mantle move the continents?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists agree that the mantle convects, but they still argue about how much the currents, and how much the sinking edges of plates, move the surface.

open_questions.q: Will everything in the universe one day be the same temperature?
open_questions.why_open: If heat keeps evening out, there would be no differences left to drive any flow. Some physicists call this heat death. It depends on dark energy and other things we do not yet understand.

open_questions.q: Why does a flowing, swirling fluid, like the air in a stormy sky, behave as it does?
open_questions.why_open: The equations for moving fluids are known, but nobody can fully predict a swirling, turbulent flow. It remains one of the great unsolved problems of physics.

open_questions.q: Do clouds, overall, make the Earth warmer or cooler?
open_questions.why_open: Clouds reflect sunlight, which cools, and trap heat radiation, which warms. Scientists are still working out which wins as the climate changes.

maths.context: This is about Colour Currents, where you let go of hot and warm drops of red water in a glass and time how long they take to rise. These are made-up results.
maths.problem: The hot drop reached the top in 4 seconds. The warm drop took 12 seconds. How many times as long did the warm drop take? What does that suggest about the temperature of a drop and how fast it moves?
maths.answer: 3 times as long. The hotter drop moved faster.
maths.explain: 12 divided by 4 is 3. The warm drop took 3 times as long. The hotter drop is lighter compared with the water around it, so it is pushed up faster.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one time by the other tells you how much faster one drop is, and so shows how the temperature changes the speed.

maths.context: This is about Dark, White and Shiny, where you wrap tumblers in black, white and foil and warm them in the Sun. These are made-up results.
maths.problem: Every tumbler started at 28 degrees. After 30 minutes the black tumbler read 40, the white read 33, the foil read 30 and the shaded one read 29. How many degrees did the Sun add to each wrapped tumbler, once you take away what the shaded one rose?
maths.answer: Black 11 degrees, white 4 degrees, foil 1 degree.
maths.explain: The shaded tumbler rose 29 minus 28, which is 1 degree. That much came from the warm day. Black rose 12, so the Sun added 11. White rose 5, so the Sun added 4. Foil rose 2, so the Sun added 1.
maths.why_maths: Taking away the shaded tumbler's rise shows how much of each rise was really caused by the Sun.

maths.context: This is about the Cool the Jug challenge, where you cool a jug of warm water with ice. These are made-up results.
maths.problem: A jug starts at 40 degrees. With the ice at the top, the water cools 3 degrees every 2 minutes. If it kept cooling at that rate, what would it read after 10 minutes? Why might the real number be higher?
maths.answer: 25 degrees. The real number may be higher because cooling slows down as the water gets closer to the ice's temperature.
maths.explain: 10 minutes is 5 steps of 2 minutes. 5 times 3 is 15. 40 minus 15 is 25. The real cooling slows as the difference between the water and the ice gets smaller.
maths.why_maths: Following a pattern forward lets you predict a result, and then you can compare the prediction with the real number to see what the pattern leaves out.

maths.context: This is about radiation. The Sun's heat crosses empty space as light.
maths.problem: Light travels about 300,000 kilometres every second. The Sun is about 150,000,000 kilometres away. How many seconds does the Sun's radiation take to reach us? How many minutes and seconds is that?
maths.answer: 500 seconds, which is 8 minutes and 20 seconds.
maths.explain: 150,000,000 divided by 300,000 is 500. 500 seconds is 8 minutes (480 seconds) and 20 seconds. So the Sun you see now is the Sun as it was 8 minutes and 20 seconds ago.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the distance by the speed tells you how long a journey takes, and shows that radiation crosses space very fast but not instantly.

maths.context: This is about the heat your body gives out, which you felt between your palms in the Roots practice.
maths.problem: Each person in a hall gives out about 100 watts of heat. A hall holds 40 people. How many watts is that? A room heater gives out 2,000 watts. How many room heaters is the crowd like?
maths.answer: 4,000 watts. It is like 2 room heaters.
maths.explain: 40 times 100 is 4,000 watts. 4,000 divided by 2,000 is 2. So a full hall is like two room heaters, which is why crowded rooms get hot.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying one person's heat by the number of people shows that small amounts add up to something large.

maths.context: This is about the Cool Roof challenge, where you test shoebox houses with different roofs in the Sun. These are made-up results.
maths.problem: The air outside is 32 degrees. After 30 minutes, the black-roof box reads 44 degrees, and the white-roof box reads 36 degrees. How many times as many degrees above the outside air was the black box compared with the white box?
maths.explain: The black box was 44 minus 32, which is 12 degrees above the outside air. The white box was 36 minus 32, which is 4 degrees above. 12 divided by 4 is 3.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two rises as a ratio shows how much better the white roof is, in a way that does not depend on how hot the day was.

maths.context: This is about the sea breeze, which you acted out. These are made-up times.
maths.problem: On a hot day, a sea breeze starts at 11:30 in the morning and dies away at 7:45 in the evening. For how long did it blow?
maths.explain: From 11:30 am to 7:30 pm is 8 hours. From 7:30 to 7:45 is 15 minutes more. So the sea breeze blew for 8 hours and 15 minutes.
maths.why_maths: Working out how long the wind blew shows the daily rhythm of the land warming and cooling.

roots.context: We have watched hot and cold drops move opposite ways, and felt warmth from a flame through a gap. Now we ask what these tell us about the world and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Heat has no 'up' of its own. In your glass, the hot drop rose and the cold drop sank. Gravity pulls the heavier cold water down, and that pushes the lighter hot water up. In a spacecraft, a candle flame is a ball, because warm air does not rise there.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'heat rises' as if rising were a law of heat itself. But rising is what happens when gravity pulls the cooler, heavier fluid down. Take away gravity, and heat stops rising.
deep_truth.evidence: In Colour Currents, the same glass sent a hot drop up and an ice-cold drop down. The only difference was which one was heavier than the water around it. On the space station, candle flames are round, and fans must keep the air moving.

three.who_am_i: You are a warm thing in a cooler room. You give off about as much heat as a 100 watt bulb, and a gentle column of warm air rises from your head all day.
three.what_is_life: A black kite, a vulture or an eagle can rise for an hour without a wingbeat, lifted by warm air that the ground gives them. Living beings find the flows of the world and use them.
three.what_is_this_world: The sea breeze, the monsoon, slow loops in the Earth's rock and bubbles on the Sun are all the same rise and fall, at very different sizes.

roots.thread: Where everything is the same temperature, nothing flows. Every wind, current, cloud and living body runs because two places differ in temperature. A difference is like a 'two', and the flow is the world trying to join them back into one. The Sun keeps making new differences, so the flowing never stops. Wind, rain, rivers and life are the many that come from one steady difference, kept alive by one star.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1800, the astronomer William Herschel wanted to know whether the colours in sunlight carry different amounts of heat. Most people then thought of heat as a weightless fluid, and not as anything to do with light. Herschel let sunlight pass through a glass prism, which spreads it into a rainbow. He put thermometers with blackened bulbs in the different colours. The temperature rose from violet to red. Then he did something clever. He placed a thermometer just beyond the red edge, where there was no visible light at all. It got the hottest of all. So there were invisible rays that carry heat, and they behave like light. We now call them infrared. In 1856, an American scientist named Eunice Foote showed that sunlight warms a jar of carbon dioxide more than a jar of ordinary air. A man read her paper aloud for her at a science meeting.
how_we_found_out.who: William Herschel, in 1800, and Eunice Foote, in 1856
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scientists thought heat was a weightless fluid called caloric, completely separate from light. Herschel's thermometer beyond the red end of sunlight showed that heat can travel as invisible rays, like light, and Foote's jars showed that different gases take in these rays differently.

quiz: The Sun's heat reaches us across empty space as radiation.
Radiation is invisible light-like waves that need nothing to travel through, not even air.
Heat itself only ever travels upward.
Hot air and hot water rise because they are lighter, but heat goes in every direction, even downward through a spoon.
A convection current is a loop: warm fluid rises, cools, sinks and is warmed again.
Warm fluid rises, spreads and cools, then sinks and flows back to be warmed, so the loop keeps going.
The Sun warms the air in between, and that warm air warms us.
Sunlight passes through clear air and mostly warms the ground and our skin, which then warm the air.
A white shiny roof stays cooler than a dark one because it reflects more sunlight.
Light, shiny things reflect radiation and stay cool; dark, dull things absorb it and get hot.
A sea breeze blows in the day because the sea is warmer than the land.
In the day the land warms faster, so air over it rises and cool sea air flows in.
Still air that cannot move carries heat very slowly, so it keeps places warm.
Trapped air cannot form convection currents, so a quilt full of small air pockets works as an insulator.
Opening a window in winter lets cold flow into a warm room.
There is no cold stuff. Heat flows out to the colder outside, and cold air is just air with less heat.
In a spacecraft a candle flame becomes a ball because hot air does not rise there.
Hot air rises only where gravity pulls cooler, heavier air down. With nothing falling, the flame stays a small ball.
Convection can carry heat along a solid steel rod.
Only liquids and gases can flow, so only they can carry heat by convection. A solid passes heat by conduction.
odd: Three are heat travelling as invisible rays across air or space; in the spoon, heat passes by touch from part to part.
Air, water and steam are fluids that can flow and carry heat by convection; a steel rod is a solid.
White, shiny and light things reflect most sunlight and stay cool; a dark, dull road absorbs it and gets hot.
Warm fluids expand and become lighter, so they rise; cold air is heavier and sinks.
Sand, rock and bare ground warm up fast in the Sun, while sea water warms much more slowly.
